Sources indicate that the most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:.

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:.

Industry observers note that the "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

According to recent reports, these definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

Industry observers note that national income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

According to recent reports, A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Recent findings suggest that income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

Industry observers note that the FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

In a recent development, what distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

Sources indicate that the distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

According to recent reports, whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Sources indicate that divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most crucial predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

In a recent development, according to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Sources indicate that upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, Latest York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

Sources indicate that the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

In a recent development, pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

In a recent development, income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L. Kang asthe winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award during a ceremony on Saturday (14 November). The Toronto-born, New York-based photographer, sculptor and installation artist won the 23rd edition of the annual award, the most high-profile and lucrative prize devoted to Canadian contemporary artists, and will receive C$100,000 ($70,000).

The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).

Industry observers note that in a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”. He continued: “Through installations using unfixed photographic film, cast and found objects, and fabricated armatures, her practice resists the stabilising impulses traditionally associated with photography. Reoccurring motifs including lotus root, flowers, soju bottles, birds, anchovies, are not fixed objects, but repositories of place, longing and desire.”.

Partial view of Lotus L. Kang's installation In Cascades (2023-24) in Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing at the Whitney Museum of American Art Photo: The Art Newspaper.

According to recent reports, kang, a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2024 whose work was included in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and the 2025 Shanghai Biennale, works across sculpture, photography and site-responsive installation. Her materially dense, non-linear installations explore the liminal space between industrial and architectural forms, familial and social histories, as well as poetry and non-human figures. One of her celebrated installation works, Mother (2020), comprised dozens of metal mixing bowls filled with scattered abstract clay, rubber and stone sculptures as well as aluminium casts of fruit and anchovies. Her critically acclaimed solo exhibition at 52 Walker in Newly introduced York last year featured several greenhouse installations as well as one made of strips of film extended around a spinning rotary dryer.

“It is an honour to be recognised by this prize,” Kang stated in a statement. “I am grateful to those I love, those who love me and those who have supported me; you keep me going. The recognition of this prize means that askew ideas are worth pursuing. Art is essential to life, progress and love.”.

During the ceremony, Kang told those assembled at the NGC and those watching via livestream: “I just want to congratulate the other artists. It’s an honour to be nominated alongside you. Shane, Melaw, Caroline, Audie, Samuel. It is really inspiring to be showing alongside you, and who knows what would have happened, and I’m just glad we’ll all keep making art, because it’s really the best thing. So, thank you so much.’’.

Lotus L. Kang, Receiver Transmitter (49 Echoes I), 2022-25 © Lotus Kang. Photo: Courtesy of the artist and 52 Walker gallery, Latest York.

Recent findings suggest that rob Sobey, the chair of the Sobey Art Foundation, offered his “heartfelt congratulations” to Kang and added: “We also celebrate tonight all 29 artists on this year’s longlist and shortlist for their creativity and vision. We are proud to champion their work and grateful to the National Gallery of Canada for helping bring these remarkable artistic voices to audiences at home and around the world.”.

Recent findings suggest that selected by an independent jury of curators and cultural leaders, Kang was chosen following a rigorous review process. The jury, who evaluated the artists’ practices, achievements, and contributions to contemporary art in Canada included Kimberly Phillips, the director of the Marianne and Edward Gibson Art Museum at Simon Fraser University, representing the Pacific region;Daisy Desrosiers, a curator at large for North America at Tate, representing the Quebec region;and Helen Nisbet, the director of Glasgow International, serving as international juror.

Works by all six shortlisted artists are currently featured in the 2026 Sobey Art Award Exhibition at the NGC in Ottawa (until 3 January 2027).

The late Frank H. Sobey, an enthusiastic collector of Canadian art, established the Sobey Art Foundation in 1981 and the Sobey Art Award was introduced in 2002. Five years ago, the award’s criteria were amended from a prize devoted to “emerging artists” under 40 to recognising artists of any age who are at a “critical juncture” in their careers. Past winners have included Brian Jungen (in 2002), Annie Pootoogook (2006), Abbas Akhavan (2015), Laakkuluk Williamson Bathory (2021) and Nico Williams (2024).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast. He’s spent years building everything from crypto … More about Mikhail ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

It has been revealed that we know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working.

According to recent reports, that gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable.

Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem.

In a recent development, this is not an article about compliance checklists or end-of-project audits. It’s about engineering systems. Specifically, why accessibility should be treated as an operational capability — alongside privacy, security, reliability, and observability — and what that looks like in practice.

It has been revealed that for years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into.

According to recent reports, audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR, you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well.

But audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple newly introduced features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way.

Recent findings suggest that the WebAIM Million report, which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and ‘vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds.

Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose.

With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies.

Start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you “fully give in to the vibes” and “forget that the code even exists”. You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated.

Sources indicate that models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And is fewer tokens than , so absent a constraint, the model takes the cheap path.

Here’s the thing about AI-generated UI: it’s inaccessible by default. Not occasionally — by default. A developer writing in Frontend Masters tested AI-generated React components across multiple tools and documented the pattern. A typical AI-generated sidebar had ten distinct accessibility failures in twenty-nine lines: no landmark, no heading, no list structure, elements with click handlers instead of buttons, no aria-expanded, no keyboard handling, and unlabeled icons. The accessibility tree — the structure screen readers actually read — came back as flat, unstructured text. “Same pixels” as the author put it. “One is a door. The other is a painting of a door”.

Industry observers note that now connect this to security, because the two failures come from the same root. Veracode’s 2025 GenAI Code Security Report tested large language models across dozens of coding tasks and found that a large fraction of AI-generated code introduced security vulnerabilities — including OWASP Top 10 flaws. Cross-site scripting failures were particularly common, and security performance did not meaningfully improve with newer, larger models. The issue wasn’t model intelligence. It was process: developers generating code without specifying security constraints and accepting output without systematic verification.

Industry observers note that the same shortcut that skips the security review skips the accessibility review. At scale, AI won’t close the accessibility gap — it has industrialized the very thing that creates it.

In a recent development, the fix is not to ban AI. Your developers are already using it. The fix is to constrain it and verify it — to treat AI as a very fast teammate who always needs guardrails.

Recent findings suggest that this is usually where someone claims, “Guardrails? Sounds great, but they will slow us down.”.

In practice, the opposite tends to be true.

Shift-left is the entire DevOps thesis, and it applies cleanly here. An accessibility issue caught during design review is a comment. The same issue found in production is a remediation project.

Catching an accessibility matter as a component is built takes minutes. Fixing one after the fact — discovering it in an audit, diagnosing the root cause, restructuring the markup, applying the necessary fix, writing tests — can easily take hours. Multiply that across hundreds of findings from a late-stage audit, and you have weeks of unplanned work that earlier automated checks — whether in design reviews, development workflows, or CI — could have prevented.

According to recent reports, teams that integrate accessibility into everyday workflows avoid the expensive surprises: emergency audits, remediation sprints, procurement blockers, and redesigns that quietly break core user journeys. Accessibility doesn’t reduce velocity. Unexpected work reduces velocity. In-flow accessibility is one way of eliminating unexpected work.

In a recent development, the organizations that scale accessibility successfully do not rely on heroes. They rely on systems.

It has been revealed that the highest-leverage place to start is the design system. One accessible component can be reused thousands of times. The GOV.UK Design System is a useful example: components undergo both automated and manual testing using assistive technologies such as JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack. The team is explicit about the limits of automation and supplements tooling with user testing involving people with disabilities. They’re equally clear that using the design system doesn’t “magically” make a service accessible; it just gives you a higher starting point.

It has been revealed that accessibility becomes infrastructure. That’s the lesson.

From there, it moves into the engineering workflow:.

Finally, accessibility becomes enforceable through automation:.

At that point, accessibility stops depending on memory and starts depending on the process. It becomes part of your platform.

A few implementation patterns consistently show up in teams that do this well.

Industry observers note that instead of fixing accessibility after generation, bake requirements directly into tooling through Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, or repository-level standards. Tell the model to use semantic HTML. Tell it when to use buttons versus links. Tell it to expose the state and labels correctly. Models follow persistent constraints far more reliably than one-off prompts.

In a recent development, comboboxes, menus, tabs, modals, and similar controls routinely become accessibility hotspots. Libraries such as Radix UI, React Aria, and Headless UI already solve many of these problems. The scalable approach is not about repeatedly implementing accessibility correctly. It’s inheriting accessible behavior from well-tested primitives.

Focus order, labels, heading hierarchy, and interaction states should be specified before implementation begins. If accessibility requirements are absent from the design artifact, they are often absent from the final product. A simple memo at design handoff — what is the tab order, what are the labels, what happens on error — removes a huge amount of guesswork later.

In a recent development, none of these patterns is exotic. They’re just DevOps and platform thinking applied to accessibility.

Industry observers note that engineering leaders rarely prioritize accessibility solely because of regulations. But regulations, procurement requirements, user retention, and product quality all point in the same direction.

According to recent reports, legal pressure continues to increase. Digital accessibility lawsuits in the United States have stayed in the thousands per year, and they are not limited to large enterprises. The European Accessibility Act is now enforceable across the EU, applying to e‑commerce, banking, ticketing, telecoms, and more, regardless of where the company is headquartered. The message is clear: accessibility is no longer a “nice-to-have” in the eyes of regulators.

In a recent development, but compliance is only part of the story. The bigger story is the market you leave on the table. The World Economic Forum (December 2023) estimates that the world’s 1.3 billion people with disabilities, “along with their friends and family, has a spending power of $13 trillion”; disabled consumers alone control roughly $8 trillion in annual disposable income, per the Valuable 500.

In the UK alone, the Click-Away Pound Report 2019 found the “Click-Away Pound has risen to £17.1 billion” — more than 4.9 million people with access needs who abandon inaccessible sites and spend elsewhere, up almost 45% from £11.75 billion in 2016. People don’t file a bug report. They leave and buy from a competitor.

There is also a procurement reality that turns accessibility from a cost into a moat. If you sell B2B or to government, you will increasingly be asked for proof of accessibility — VPATs/ACRs or equivalent documentation. According to Level Access’s Seventh Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report, 75% of organizations now require proof of accessibility at least most of the time when purchasing digital products — essentially unchanged from 74% in the previous report, but with a notable shift towards stricter enforcement, as those that always require it rose from 27% to 31%. A strong ACR accelerates the sales cycle; a weak one, or none at all, creates redlines that stall or kill it. For some buyers, this is a hard requirement before your product can even enter evaluation. A strong accessibility story accelerates the sales cycle. A weak one creates redlines that stall or kill it.

Step back and the deeper pattern is clear: accessibility is a proxy for engineering maturity. A team that ships semantic HTML, manages focus, exposes state correctly, and tests it in CI is a team that has its house in order. The same discipline that produces an accessible component produces a maintainable, testable, less buggy one.

It has been revealed that for dev and product leaders, that’s the real business case: accessibility work is platform work. It pays off every time a feature ships faster and more smoothly, with less rework, than it otherwise would have.

It has been revealed that if you take one thing from this, make it this: accessibility doesn’t come from an audit, a hero, or a heroic remediation sprint before launch. It comes from systems.

An accessible design system so components start right. A Definition of Done so they stay right. Automated testing and CI gates so regressions fail the build. Governance, so someone owns it. Guardrails for AI-assisted development so your fastest tool stops being your biggest liability.

Recent findings suggest that none of those practices is particularly glamorous. That’s exactly why they work. They’re the same kinds of boring, reliable systems you already trust for security, reliability, and performance.

But there’s one thing no tool on that list can do. No linter, no automated scanner run, no dashboard will ever tell you what it’s actually like to use your product as a blind person with a screen reader, or to navigate your checkout with a keyboard because a tremor makes a mouse inoperable. So build the systems — you need them, and they’re the only way accessibility survives contact with a real release schedule. But test with real owners with disabilities regularly. The first time you sit behind someone using JAWS to fight through a form your team thought was “done”, something changes. The tooling tells you whether you passed. A real person tells you whether it actually works.

Sources indicate that accessibility is not a feature. It’s an operational capability. Treat it that way, and you get something dev and product leaders already care about: a faster, safer, more reliable way to ship software.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In a recent development, the design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, the design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on dialogue, the industry has collectively decided that the chat bubble is the natural home for every AI capability. While the chat interface is a viable and powerful option for many tasks, it is one tool in an expansive toolkit. UX and Product teams must be intentional about the modalities we choose for how users provide their data and commands, and how the system presents its output.

Recent findings suggest that to pick the best method, you need to think about what the user wants to do, where they are, and how much cognitive effort they are already expending. This guide offers a clear way to figure out the best approach for any product, using two tools to assist in the process: a Task Audit and an Input/Output Alignment Matrix.

Picture a traveler jogging through a loud airport terminal after a sudden gate change. They are dragging their roller bag and carrying a coffee in the other hand. They need to open their airline app to ask the AI assistant where to go. The tool immediately fails the input modality test. It forces the traveler to stop walking, balance their coffee, and type a long booking reference number into a tiny chat box. When they finally hit send, the system fails the output modality test. Instead of flashing a large, high-contrast gate number, the AI returns a dense paragraph explaining the atmospheric weather patterns causing the delay. The actual gate number sits buried at the very bottom.

While they might make the flight just fine, the user won’t forget the moment of anxiety they felt while using the AI tool — an experience that could have served as a way to reinforce a commitment to UX has instead validated the common conception that companies don’t care about or understand customers using their products. In this scenario, the airline built a smart tool, but the interface failed the user. The input required physical dexterity, which the traveler lacked at the time of need. The output demanded a level of reading focus they could not spare. This article will cover how we can avoid this scenario in our AI-powered tools. In order to be successful, we must evaluate the physical and cognitive load of our people to match both the input and output modality to their immediate intent.

Let’s first discuss the limitations of a chat-based interface.

It has been revealed that the allure of the chatbot is easy to understand from a product development standpoint. It is a blank slate. It suggests that the system can handle anything the user provides. However, a text-heavy interface often causes a high adaptation load. This load increases cognitive demands on people. Over time, this cognitive burden turns into a psychological tax a person pays when changing natural thought processes to accommodate a machine.

Sources indicate that when an interface relies solely on conversation, it imposes a dual burden: a linguistic challenge for input and a cognitive challenge for output. We’ll examine both separately below.

In a recent development, A blank chat box creates a major problem for people who need to discover what a tool can actually do. In a standard graphical interface, menus and buttons provide clear visual cues that signal every available option. A chat box often leads to choice paralysis because users are forced to guess what the AI is capable of. They have to remember the exact phrasing or technical terms required to get the result they want.

Consider a data analyst who wants to find a specific trend in a spreadsheet. In a traditional tool, they might click a filter or sort button. In a chat interface, they must suddenly become a writer and describe that complex logic in a complete sentence. Another example: a manager trying to reorganize a team schedule. Dragging and dropping blocks on a calendar is intuitive. Describing those same scheduling shifts in a text prompt adds a layer of work that makes the task feel more difficult than it should be.

Designing for input means recognizing that composing a prompt is a creative act. It requires a person to translate a vague thought into a specific command. For many professionals, this creates a linguistic barrier. A designer might know exactly how they want an image to look but struggle to describe the lighting or texture in a text prompt. In that case, a slider or a color picker is a much better input method than a text box.

Sources indicate that having addressed the linguistic barrier of constructing input prompts, we must now consider the other half of the conversational burden. This is the cognitive cost the AI imposes when it responds in dense blocks of text.

When an AI responds in long blocks of text, it transfers the interpretive work to you, the user. Text is a serial medium: your brain has to read one word after the next to extract meaning. That takes time. Sequential reading is necessary in many scenarios. Complex legal analysis or reviewing nuanced medical histories requires reading full paragraphs. Teams create friction when they default to text for data that visual formats communicate faster. Visual methods allow parallel processing. You can view a chart and spot a pattern in under a second.

Recent findings suggest that imagine asking an AI for a project status upgrade. Instead of a color-coded dashboard, you receive three paragraphs listing every task completed that week. Now you must read the entire response and mentally summarize it to find the one piece of information you needed. The quick visual check has been replaced by a reading assignment.

The cognitive tax of this work compounds with professional stakes. A doctor asking for a patient’s vital signs needs a clear numerical display, not a narrative describing the readings. A stock trader looking for a price spike needs a line graph immediately, not a written description of price movement over the past hour. In both cases, a text response forces the professional through a slow, error-prone extraction process when speed and accuracy are most important.

Industry observers note that before selecting a modality, practitioners need a shared vocabulary for what the options actually are. The table below maps common input and output modalities to the contexts where each performs best. This is not a ranking. Each modality has a role; the question is always which role it is playing in a given workflow.

According to recent reports, designing for modality inherently requires a strong focus on accessibility. While visual dashboards provide rapid insight for many people, designers need to provide screen-reader-optimized audio alternatives for users with visual disabilities. Modality choices should multiply pathways to information.

Table 1: Input and Output Modality Taxonomy. Use this as a reference during the Task Audit to identify candidate modalities before narrowing to a recommendation.

It has been revealed that the following FigureFigure 2 illustrates the cognitive spectrum, mapping how mental effort scales across various interaction methods. This spectrum is a critical tool for designers to visualize the shift from low-effort, ambient interactions to high-effort, focused experiences. By understanding where a specific task sits on this spectrum, teams can identify whether a user needs a “glanceable” output that minimizes mental processing or a high-density format that supports deep, analytical thinking.

Recent findings suggest that with this taxonomy established, the next step is to apply a rigorous method to select the optimal input and output combination. Practitioners must ground this selection process in the user’s real-world environment and context.

According to recent reports, to choose the right interaction method, practitioners should complete a Task Audit before interface design begins. A formal Task Audit is the framework that moves teams from assumptions about user behavior to evidence. This process gathers data about the physical, social, and cognitive context in which the work actually happens, which then drives all input and output modality decisions.

Use these four areas of focus to anchor the audit:.

The audit answers two questions for every feature:.

It has been revealed that here is how to gather the evidence to inform your task audit. Use one or more of these common UX research-related methods:.

Sources indicate that this is the most direct way to capture how people work in their natural setting, and it provides the richest data for identifying physical constraints on both input and output. Observation is necessary because owners often perform hidden work: small steps or workarounds they forget to mention in an interview, or environmental details they do not think to describe because they have adapted to them.

Recent findings suggest that the Approach: Go to the user’s actual workspace, whether a field site, warehouse, or office floor. Ask them to perform the task you are studying and observe closely.

What to Look For: This method is most revealing for Input Constraints and Output Constraints.

In a recent development, interviews surface the mental models and decision points that observation cannot capture. They are most valuable for understanding Cognitive Load.

The Approach: Conduct one-on-one sessions with end-consumers and the stakeholders who manage the outcome. Use a structured protocol focused on a specific task. Ask for stories about past successes and failures rather than general opinions.

Industry observers note that workshops are essential for defining task boundaries and establishing required fidelity levels. Product managers and stakeholders bring foundational knowledge of system requirements; researchers apply audit criteria.

The Approach: Use workshops to build a shared Task Inventory. Bring designers, engineers, product managers, and business analysts together to map every step of the process. Product managers and business analysts ensure factual accuracy; the research team applies audit criteria to each step.

In a recent development, once you gather field evidence through these research channels, map your findings directly against the Modality Taxonomy. Each concrete physical or social constraint you document systematically eliminates mismatched interfaces. This process strips away design guesswork, narrowing your architectural choices down to the specific input and output combinations that survive the reality of the user’s environment.

According to recent reports, when you ground input and output modality decisions in field evidence rather than interface convention, the resulting design reduces adaptation load for the user and grounds your modality choices in evidence. When you base decisions on field data, you move past interface convention and build a powerful case for the resources needed to create the right experience for your people.

Once the audit is complete, the final step is utilizing the Input/Output Alignment Matrix to formalize the connection between user intent and the optimal modality combination.

Sources indicate that with Task Audit findings in hand, you can use an Input/Output Alignment Matrix to map user intent to specific modality combinations. This matrix is organized by what the user is trying to accomplish in a given moment. This distinction versus focusing on what your AI is capable of doing matters. If intent changes across a single workday for the same user, the interface should respond to those shifts.

Recent findings suggest that choosing the wrong modality for the user’s context can lead to user frustration. Users might feel mentally drained if a lot of information is delivered through a format that is hard to process, like getting a massive status patch only in text. They may also start worrying if an action was actually completed correctly when a precise command is buried within a long chat exchange. Finally, the system can force users into finding clumsy workarounds, making them adapt to the machine’s method instead of working in their natural, most effective way.

Table 2: Input/Output Alignment Matrix. Map user intent to modality combinations using Task Audit evidence. The two added rows (Monitoring/Alert and Guided Task Completion) cover common enterprise and mobile scenarios not captured in simpler frameworks.

When teams coordinate these factors, they can move past the automatic default of adding a chatbot. Visual layouts enable rapid scanning. Structured inputs remove the burden of constructing perfect sentences. Audio outputs serve owners whose hands and eyes are otherwise occupied.

A real-world scenario where environmental constraints dictated a shift in design strategy best demonstrates the practical application of this matrix and the broader audit framework.

Sources indicate that field technicians servicing high-voltage electrical grids often face a dangerous misalignment of interface modality. Traditionally, these technicians had to rely on ruggedized tablets to access technical manuals and log status updates. However, the physical constraints of the job — wearing heavy protective gloves and working in bucket trucks at significant heights — made interacting with a standard touch interface nearly impossible while on a job site. Additionally, attempting to read complex, text-heavy diagnostic reports on a screen while maintaining situational awareness created a high cognitive load that increased the risk of safety errors.

To address this, researchers conducted a Task Audit utilizing three specific methods from this article. First, Contextual Inquiry and Observation revealed that technicians often worked in “hands-busy, eyes-busy” states where any manual input was a significant barrier. Researchers observed technicians wearing mandatory thick protective gloves while in the bucket truck, which made precise screen taps nearly impossible and often triggered the wrong commands.

High-altitude environments also introduced severe screen glare from direct sunlight, washing out the display and making text difficult to read even at full brightness. Furthermore, technicians faced the physical safety risk of trying to manipulate and secure a heavy, ruggedized tablet while balanced in awkward positions, creating a distraction that could lead to dangerous slips or equipment contact. These factors, combined with the need to constantly monitor live wires and the surrounding environment, meant technicians could not safely dedicate their eyes or hands to a standard tablet interface, confirming the severity of the eyes-busy and hands-busy constraints.

According to recent reports, second, Focused Interviews with veteran technicians validated the findings from the field. They confirmed that the operational challenges, including the thick gloves, screen glare, and safety risks, were not unique to one location but were commonly experienced across multiple sites, including high-altitude transmission lines and sprawling power substations. This broad confirmation solidified the need for a non-touch, voice-first solution. The interviews also surfaced a critical cognitive constraint: the need for glance verification of vital signs, such as voltage readings and temperature trends, rather than being forced to read a long narrative description of system health. Technicians stressed that their primary need was immediate, unambiguous verification (is this safe? or where is the fault?), not a lengthy diagnostic report, indicating that a text-heavy response was dangerous to their workflow.

These methods confirmed that the environment required a departure from the traditional chat or form-based AI capability interface.

In a recent development, the resulting solution implemented an adaptive modality handoff designed to mitigate the physical and cognitive barriers researchers identified during the research. While active on a job site, technicians utilize voice input to query the system. This method allows them to remain productive while wearing thick protective gloves that would otherwise prevent precise interaction with a touchscreen.

The AI responds with a short audio summary of immediate diagnostic data. This audio feedback bypasses the challenge of screen glare in high-altitude environments and allows the technician to maintain situational awareness of the high-voltage grid without the safety risk of looking away from dangerous equipment. By providing immediate answers to fault locations through audio, the system meets the technician’s need for glance verification through a hands-free and eyes-free channel.

Recent findings suggest that once technicians return to a truck and secure safety gear, a system automatically hands off workflows to a 15-inch visual dashboard mounted inside a vehicle. A rugged 10-inch field tablet lacks adequate screen real estate for complex schematics. A larger vehicle display allows for parallel processing of historical trend data and wide electrical grid maps. This case study reflects an actual field audit conducted for a national utility provider. Implementing this adaptive approach reduced diagnostic time by twenty percent and increased daily tool adoption among field crews.

According to recent reports, an AI capability is only as usable as the interface that delivers it. Researchers and designers must resist the pull toward the path of least resistance. Building a chatbot is fast and familiar, something we’ve been doing for decades now. Building an interface that feels like a natural extension of how someone already works is harder, and it is the work that matters.

Start by leaving the screen. The Task Audit requires presence in the places where work actually happens: the field site, the warehouse floor, the operating room. The physical and social realities of those spaces are not edge cases. They are the design brief.

The future of AI interface design is a diverse ecosystem: visual, vocal, haptic, and ambient, calibrated to user intent and environmental context. The chat window is one tool in that ecosystem. It is the right tool for specific jobs, and often the wrong tool for the jobs we reflexively assign to it.

To get started immediately, run a lightweight version of the Task Audit before your next design sprint. Spend two hours observing the workflow in its actual environment. Conduct three to five interviews with the people who perform the task. Bring a PM or analyst into a 90-minute workshop to build a task inventory and apply the four audit questions. You will not have complete data, but you will have enough to make a defensible modality recommendation backed by evidence rather than convention.

According to recent reports, I created a Modality Task Audit Template to help guide teams with moving forward. You can download this worksheet and take it directly to your next field observation. It allows design and product teams to document specific physical barriers before writing a single line of code.

We focus heavily on training smarter AI models. We owe equal attention to human interfaces. A brilliant underlying model packaged in a lazy text interface fails. When you observe actual work environments and align interaction modalities to them, you remove adaptation friction.

According to recent reports, use this worksheet during field observations. It allows design teams to document specific physical barriers before writing code.

Observe customers as they perform a primary task in actual workspaces. Check all applicable conditions.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom.
  • “Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” says the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte.
  • Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom. One such building is the decommissioned Terminal 1 of Zayed International Airport, which was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 1982. Now a designated heritage site, it is the unique venue for the Abu Dhabi edition of the itinerant art and design fair Nomad (18-22 November), which returns to the city for a second time in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism.

“Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” says the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte. “[Terminal 1] has a very particular architecture, but also a history as a place of movement and exchange. Rather than placing conventional booths inside it, we wanted to work with the building as we found it—its terminals, corridors, scale and different spatial conditions—and allow those qualities to become part of how the works are experienced.”.

Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.

This year, the fair is expanding that mission with ambitious site-specific takeovers of four of the airport’s private terminals by Nilufar gallery, Gallery Fumi, Galerie Gastou and the jewellery advisory firm A2Z. There are 50 exhibitors taking part this year (compared with 40 last year) including local returning participants such as Leila Heller Gallery and the A/P Room as well as international spaces like Paris-based Galerie BSL, Milan’s Galleria Rossana Orlandi and Carpenters Workshop Gallery from London.

Highlights at the fair will include Maison Intègre’s bronze objects made using the ancient technique of lost wax, cast from recycled metal at its foundry in Burkina Faso; Seoul-based gallery Vein’s pairing of contemporary Korean practices with traditions including ottchil lacquer and mother-of-pearl inlay; and Polish design from Craftica Gallery.

Sources indicate that bellavance‑Lecompte states that jewellery will also be in the spotlight—as well as the 450 sq. m exhibition by A2Z, there will be presentations from the designers Studio Renn, Mattar jewellers and the gallery and advisory Ars Belga/Matthu-Boghossian. The Belgian jewellers Levuma will collaborate with the London gallery JCRD Design to bring together fine jewellery, diamonds and Brazilian design.

Another notable development for Nomad this year is its expanded roster of institutions and non-profit initiatives on show in the old airport’s departure hall. Joining Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council—a Sharjah-based organisation that works with female artisans from the UAE and the wider Middle East, North Africa, South and Southeast Asia regions—which returns for this edition, is the recently established Design Commission Abu Dhabi and a collaborative presentation from the Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA) in Paris and House of Artisans, a cultural centre in Abu Dhabi that preserves traditional Emirati crafts. The project will bring together the French Sudanese fashion designer Abdel El Tayeb, who won the Confirmed Talent category of IMA’s 2024 Design Prize, and Emirati artisans to create a site-specific installation. “[This project] speaks to an idea at the heart of this edition: craft is a living practice, and something newly introduced can emerge when makers from different places work together,” Bellavance‑Lecompte notes.

For Nomad’s inaugural Abu Dhabi edition, galleries reported sales exceeding $20m and many are “returning this year with more ambitious projects”, Bellavance‑Lecompte notes. He expects that Abu Dhabi’s expanding cultural calendar and soon-to-open Guggenheim museum will bring more international collectors, curators and attention to the city and to Nomad. “Last year showed us that there is serious interest in collectable design, and this year we can build on those relationships,” he says.

• Nomad Abu Dhabi, Old Abu Dhabi Airport, 18-22 November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.

The Purple, one of the newly introduced card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip. The same violet bleeds into a painted field behind the card, so object and world share one color. Wolff Olins spent time in Seoul before drawing anything, talking with customers and young Koreans. More than eight in ten South Koreans in their twenties still live with their parents, so people define themselves through taste and through what they choose to carry. A card notes something about who you are and who you intend to become, and that became the design problem.

In a recent development, the system runs on a simple split. A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card. Around that core, each card gets its own world. The entry cards, M, X and Z, use a generative system of bright color and repetition, so no two faces repeat the same pattern. A type specimen sheet sets the grotesque in full, and the card specification drawing marks the 1.58 ratio every face must hold.

In a recent development, scale does the talking in the applications. The wordmark stays small and bracketed while a single figure, 93 percent, fills a whole green panel, and the card faces run at poster size on street walls. The card ratio repeats across posters, totes and packaging, so the system reads as one object cut to different sizes.

The physical pieces carry the same discipline. Modular packaging holds the whole range together: a grey box with a debossed Hyundai Card mark and a red peel tab, each card sealed in a protective layer that peels back to reveal its character. The dotted halftone on the Purple card reads as texture before it reads as pattern. The tote bag carries the bracketed wordmark on green, with a black band at the base.

Color is the flex in the system. Violet owns the Purple card, acid green owns the commercial card and the significant figures, and black and grey hold everything together. The butterfly image shows what the generative color does when it leaves the card: the same violet, painted loose across a wing, with the pattern breaking into dots. Every card keeps the same bones and gets a different skin.

Customers Don’t Need More Tools: They Need Seamless Integrations

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • We often hear about shiny new tools that change everything (yet again).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

We often hear about shiny new tools that change everything (yet again). But in practice, most people don’t need more tools to deal with in their daily lives. What we actually need are better integrations of useful capabilities that neatly align with our existing and established mental models.

It has been revealed that users don’t get excited about shiny upcoming “smart” workflows, or navigating Terminal commands, or jumping between endless back-and-forth chat interactions. They need seamless integrations of useful features to address problems with high severity, high frequency, and a high level of frustration.

In a recent development, I’ve always been puzzled by the notion of “AI-first” products. They might speed up production, but we need to know really well first what we actually want to build. AI-first often doesn’t account for years of small and big design decisions that have shaped expectations and mental models over the years.

I love the notion of “Quiet AI”. These are tools that are mostly invisible, sit in the background, and do small tasks on the user’s behalf. They never scream for attention but happily assist in repetitive, frustrating tasks that can easily be automated or assisted with a smart helper.

Excellent examples of Quiet AI include Claude’s integration within Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, providing assistance in context without disrupting the user’s workflow.

According to recent reports, so no wonder that I absolutely love the idea of folder instructions! There, people can define what a folder is supposed to do, based on the purpose they created it for. It sounds much more complicated than it actually is.

According to recent reports, the instructions define what the folder is for, how files should be organized, how sub-folders should behave, and what actions can happen inside. Instead of manually maintaining a folder, you set its intent once and let the system follow it.

According to recent reports, it’s a seamless integration of AI helpers just when and where owners want and need it. With permissions and actions locally scoped to that specific folder on the user’s machine, unless the user extends access, permissions, or system rules on their own.

Note: For a deeper dive into this concept, you can jump to Karthikeya GS’s wonderful post “Folder Instructions: Instructions For System-Level AI”.

It has been revealed that user’s value doesn’t emerge from people having to juggle between multiple applications, views, and sources every few minutes. That’s when they are slowed down, and that’s when they make mistakes.

It comes from helping users do the work they need to do — by reducing frustrations, slowdowns and mistakes, and taking care of tasks that otherwise would take too much time and too much effort to complete well.

Yet again, seamless integrations — a very underused but incredibly impactful way to deliver value fast, without adding the burden of installing and learning yet another tool.

The Best Tech Gifts for Design Enthusiasts

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that for this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do.
  • According to recent reports, the boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it. But look beyond the specifications, and you’ll find plenty of objects worth paying attention to: a clock that uses light and sound to mark the passing hours, a digital frame that resembles a printed photograph, and a cassette-playing boombox that brings back the pleasure of physical controls.

Industry observers note that for this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do. Some embrace the past, others experiment with upcoming technology, and a few make the everyday business of charging, organizing, and staying connected a little more enjoyable.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store.

According to recent reports, the boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters. Studebaker’s retro-inspired design brings the 1980s into the present with Bluetooth connectivity, a CD player, USB playback, and a cassette deck that can even record music. A rechargeable battery and built-in carrying handle make it easy to take the nostalgia wherever the party goes.

The SB214OS Bluetooth Boombox is available at store.moma.org for $250.

Photography courtesy of Polaroid.

Industry observers note that polaroid’s Mod puts creative controls directly on the camera, inviting experimentation without the distraction of a smartphone screen. Dedicated physical controls make it easy to explore effects like double exposures, light painting, motion freeze, and split-shot compositions. It’s a refreshingly hands-on approach to photography that encourages a little spontaneity and plenty of happy accidents.

The Polaroid Mod Instant Camera is available at polaroid.com for $169.99.

Photography courtesy of Therabody.

Industry observers note that therabody takes a different approach to workout recovery with a device designed to fit between your hands. To help manage body heat during workouts, the handheld device uses temperature-controlled surfaces to cool both palms simultaneously, with additional heat and contrast therapy settings. Compact and cordless, it provides an alternative to ice baths and other more cumbersome temperature-based recovery equipment.

The CryoTherm Palm is available at therabody.com for $399.99.

Photography courtesy of Balmuda.

Sources indicate that inspired by traditional pocket watches, Balmuda’s The Clock reimagines how we experience time through light, sound, and movement. Its carved aluminum body houses 75 LEDs that create an animated display, while built-in speakers play ambient soundscapes designed for focus, relaxation, and sleep. With customizable alarms, app connectivity, and USB-C charging, it’s a thoughtful alternative to the conventional bedside clock.

The Clock is available at us.balmuda.com for $499 in Silver and $519 in Champagne.

Photography courtesy of Bang & Olufsen.

Bang & Olufsen’s Beoplay H100 headphones are undeniably a splurge, but they’re designed with longevity in mind. The Danish brand developed the H100 with replaceable components, including the ear cushions, headband, and batteries. The custom titanium drivers, soft leather detailing, and rich color options give them a distinctly luxurious feel, while advanced noise cancellation and immersive sound make the listening experience just as considered as the design. It’s an investment piece for someone who appreciates exceptional craftsmanship as much as great audio.

The Beoplay H100 Headphones are available at bang-olufsen.com for $2,200.

Photography courtesy of Warby Parker.

Smart glasses are getting a stylish update thanks to Warby Parker’s collaboration with Google and Samsung. Available in three of the brand’s familiar silhouettes, the lightweight frames incorporate a camera, open-ear speakers, and Gemini AI for hands-free photography, calls, navigation, and more. Subtly translucent temples offer a glimpse of the technology inside without compromising the classic eyewear design. With prescription, nonprescription, reading, and sunglass options, they’re a surprisingly versatile gift.

Intelligent Eyewear is available for preorder at warbyparker.com, starting at $395.

Photography courtesy of Flowtica.

What looks like an ordinary ballpoint pen has a few technological tricks up its sleeve. The Flowtica Scribe combines a functional writing instrument with an AI-powered voice recorder, allowing users to capture conversations while taking notes on paper the old-fashioned way. A companion app can transcribe recordings and turn them into summaries and action items, bringing digital convenience to a familiar analog tool. An optional vegan leather charging case gives the device a place to rest between meetings.

The Flowtica Scribe is available at flowtica.ai for $159.

Photography courtesy of Bellroy.

Anyone who’s ever untangled a mess of charging cables at the bottom of a bag will appreciate Bellroy’s thoughtfully designed Tech Kit. The small organizer opens flat to reveal a series of mesh pockets and elastic loops that keep chargers, cables, earbuds, and other tech essentials neatly in place. Its structured shape makes everything easy to see and access, while the streamlined exterior, made from recycled woven fabric, slips neatly into a backpack or carry-on. It’s a simple solution to one of travel’s most persistent little annoyances.

The Tech Kit is available at bellroy.com for $59–$69, depending on color.

Amazon’s latest Kindle redesign brings a more refined look and feel to the familiar e-reader. The Paperwhite Signature Edition pairs a sleek aluminum body with a 7-inch, glare-free display, adjustable warm lighting, and double-tap page turning. Waterproof construction and wireless charging make it an easy travel companion, while two finishes, Graphite and Seaglass Green, offer a choice between classic and colorful.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is available at amazon.com for $250.

Photography courtesy of Daily Objects.

Who says charging stations have to be boring? DailyObjects’ Surge Foldaway turns an everyday tech essential into a sculptural desktop accessory. Its adjustable design accommodates an iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods simultaneously, consolidating three charging spots into one tidy footprint. The bold Cosmic Orange finish adds a welcome pop of color, giving the accessory a presence even when the devices are elsewhere.

The Surge Foldaway 3-in-1 Wireless Charger is available at dailyobjects.us for $175.

Photography courtesy of ModRetro.

A love letter to handheld gaming, ModRetro’s Chromatic brings the original Game Boy experience into the present with a few thoughtful upgrades. Its magnesium-alloy body houses a custom, pixel-perfect display designed to play original Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges. The colorful finishes include four translucent options that expose the internal hardware, turning the console’s components into part of its visual identity.

The Chromatic + Tetris Bundle is available at modretro.com starting at $199.

Shark’s CryoGlow Plus combines two skincare technologies in a single wearable device: LED light therapy and under-eye cooling. Red, blue, and infrared lights power several treatment modes, while adjustable cooling pads help refresh tired eyes. The upgraded design offers improved LED coverage around the eyes and mouth, and the soft Pastel Berry finish makes this wearable gadget surprisingly stylish.

The CryoGlow Plus LED Face Mask is available at sharkninja.com for $379.99.

Sources indicate that in a market crowded with phones competing for attention, the Mudita Kompakt is designed to demand less of it. Its minimalist design centers on a 4.3-inch E Ink display, favoring a restrained interface over colorful notifications and app-heavy screens. Essential features like calling, messaging, offline maps, and a camera remain, while a dedicated offline switch offers a physical way to disconnect.

The Mudita Kompakt is available at mudita.com for $399.

Who claims smart technology has to look high-tech? Birdfy’s Feeder Wood combines the charm of a traditional wooden birdhouse with a built-in camera, letting bird lovers watch their feathered visitors up close. Made from FSC-certified wood, the solar-powered feeder captures 1080p video. Its companion app can identify more than 6,000 bird species, bringing a layer of digital discovery to an otherwise familiar backyard ritual.

The Feeder Wood is available at birdfy.com for $189.99.

Sources indicate that wallie’s approach to the digital photo frame starts with a simple idea: make the screen look less like a screen. Its 10-inch color E Ink display gives photographs the appearance of printed images, while real wood construction and a choice of four finishes help it blend into a gallery wall or shelf arrangement. Rounded or square corners offer further customization, and a rechargeable battery eliminates the need for a visible power cord. Photos can be updated remotely through an app.

The Wallie 10 is available at shop.wallieframe.com for $299.

With its simple spherical form, Eve Flare looks more like an illuminated object than a conventional lamp. The rechargeable, water-resistant light offers millions of customizable colors, with app and voice controls for setting the mood indoors or outside. Its wireless charging base and portable design mean it can move effortlessly from a bedside table to the patio, adding a little atmosphere wherever it lands.

The Eve Flare Portable Smart LED Lamp is available at apple.com for $99.95.

Photography courtesy of Best Buy.

8BitDo borrows the visual language of the original Nintendo Entertainment System for a mechanical keyboard that feels straight out of the 1980s. Chunky gray keys, red accents, and tactile mechanical switches establish the retro aesthetic, while an included joystick and two oversized programmable buttons bring arcade-style controls to the desktop. Bluetooth and wireless connectivity keep the throwback design compatible with contemporary setups.

The 8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard N Edition is available at bestbuy.com for $79.99.

Photography courtesy of Orbitkey.

Even the most organized desk tends to accumulate charging cables, adapters, and other small tech accessories. Orbitkey’s Nest v2 gives them a designated home in a compact storage box with adjustable dividers and a fabric-lined interior. The removable leather-covered lid doubles as a valet tray and 15W wireless charger, keeping everyday essentials within reach while concealing the clutter underneath.

The Nest v2 is available at orbitkey.com for $125.

Tech Report: OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made?
  • Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.
  • “Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the latest Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

Sources indicate that the architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” says Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Sources indicate that reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Industry observers note that inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

In the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

Sources indicate that the store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into newly introduced objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” claims Gianotten.

Designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

According to recent reports, “We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving new value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”.

At the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

According to recent reports, murrye Bernard is an architect-turned-writer covering architecture, interiors, product design, and sustainability. A registered architect, she has written for Architect, Architectural Record, Metropolis, Hospitality Design, Texas Architect, Green Building Advisor, and The Architect's Newspaper. She previously served as managing editor of Contract magazine and enjoys exploring the intersection of design, materials, and culture.

Seven shows to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper
