📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.
  • In What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory.
  • The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.

In What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory. Through a series of sculptural works, etchings and drawings, Al Mubarak strives to recall specific places and objects from her own childhood, embracing the distortions of memory. A monumental sandcastle evokes a child’s perspective of space, while bubble wrap that has been compulsively popped or left intact is cast in resin, turning a disposable material into an enduring sculptural form.

The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.

Emirati artist Shaikha Al Mazrou at the Cultural Foundation, where she is staging a solo show Courtesy the Cultural Foundation.

Cultural Foundation, Abu Dhabi, 12 November-15 March 2027.

Recent findings suggest that in 2022, Shaikha Al Mazrou presented her large-scale work Red Stack as part of Frieze Sculpture in London’s Regent’s Park. The work exemplifies her deft approach to defying perceptions through her choice of materials. It features a pile of red cushions constructed from fibreglass and resin on a metal framework. Despite the hardness of the materials, the creased and pillowy cushions evoke a sense of softness.

She receives her strongest spotlight to date with her solo exhibition at the Abu Dhabi’s Cultural Foundation. It will feature past work alongside upcoming commissions created specifically for the venue’s atrium. Al Mazrou’s work is also on view at Frieze Abu Dhabi with Lawrie Shabibi.

Installation view: All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, 2026. Pictured here: Rand Abdul Jabbar, Earthly Wonders, Celestial Beings (series), (2024).

NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Abu Dhabi, until 3 January 2027.

In 1951, Jewad Selim and Shakir Hassan Al Mentioned established a movement that sought to express Modernist art principles through a uniquely Iraqi perspective. It would prove to be one of the most defining moments of Arab art.

Recent findings suggest that all Manner of Experiments is perhaps the most comprehensive survey of the Baghdad Modern Art Group. It presents seminal works from the period as well as contemporary pieces that highlight the ongoing legacies of the group.

It has been revealed that the exhibition at the Newly introduced York University (NYU) Abu Dhabi Art Gallery brings together works from 1946 to 2023, from private and institutional collections. Selim’s experiments with abstraction are represented, as well as Al Said’s figurative expressions and his latter work that employed Arabic letters to convey an inner dimension. Key works by Dia al-Azzawi, Madiha Umar and Khalid al-Rahal are also presented, with the exhibition concluding with contemporary pieces by Mahmoud Obaidi, Walid Siti and Rand Abdul Jabbar, among others.

A key point of departure in this show is Selim’s Freedom Monument, a 50m-long sculpture in Tahrir Square that was commissioned just after the 1958 military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and established the Iraqi Republic. Though Selim died in 1961 before the sculpture fully materialised, it is considered to be one of his most enduring works, potent with the sensibilities that inspired the Baghdad Modern Art Group. Read from right to left—like an Arabic text—the monument tells the story of the revolution. Its bronze figures draw from Sumerian motifs while also employing Modernist aesthetics.

A carved ivory jewelled casket on show in the exhibition Spices and Wonders at Louvre Abu Dhabi © Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi; Photo: Sylvie Van Roey.

Louvre Abu Dhabi, until 14 February 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the Indian Ocean has been a pivotal node of cultural exchange for centuries, and an exhibition at the Louvre Abu Dhabi unravels the ancient maritime connections that linked Europe, Africa and the Middle East to South and Southeast Asia. Held in collaboration with the Guimet Museum in Paris, the exhibition charts these links through artefacts, textiles, ceramics and spices.

This investigation extends to Art Here—a staple show in Louvre Abu Dhabi’s calendar, presenting works shortlisted for the annual Richard Mille Art Prize. This year’s exhibition, exploring the theme of “Confluences” is curated by Kamini Sawhney (until 28 February 2027).

Serendipitously, the theme of Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi also looks towards the Indian Ocean, presenting artefacts, maps and rare books. Presentations at Frieze will contribute to research into an understudied historical topic with implications for the modern era.

Luisa Dörr, various works from Escaramuzas, (2024–ongoing).

Photography Gallery, Sharjah, until 29 November.

The 13th edition of Vantage Point takes place at the Photography Gallery in Sharjah, a venue that opened in November 2025. The exhibition, an annual fixture in Sharjah’s arts programme since 2013, is being held in an overhauled format. Each year, dozens of international artists have taken part in the exhibition, which celebrates photographic works across genres, from photojournalism to more experimental compositions. Vantage Point has now been pared down, exhibiting commissioned works by six photographers, and it will also be a biennial event moving forward.

Recent findings suggest that sathish Kumar presents a series of images that focus on his brother, an oil worker in Abu Dhabi. Photographs of Kumar’s family in the industrial city compound in Al Ruwais are juxtaposed with those taken in Bengaluru in southern India. Much of the latter centre around the construction site of the family home. The series, titled Bond, alludes to the fraught experiences of many South Asian labourers who travel to the Gulf with the aim of financially supporting their parents and families back home.

Recent findings suggest that the other works featured in the exhibition are equally evocative and personal. Latifa AlBokhari presents tender images that mark key moments in a woman’s life in the Gulf, from henna traditions to wedding preparations. Guanyu Xu shows life-sized images of domestic interiors that offer clues to the personalities of the people that inhabit them. Luisa Dörr documents with painterly sensibilities a female-focused equestrian school in Mexico. Maheder Haileselassie spotlights archival images of Arbegnoch fighters, who resisted the Italian occupation of Ethiopia between 1936 and 1941. Finally, Adam Rouhana presents larger-than-life portraits of Palestinians from the West Bank, whom he photographed in a travelling studio.

Courtesy of the artist and ATHR Gallery.

The Jameel Arts Centre has given five artists each a dedicated space within the institution.

Industry observers note that one room charts four decades of Walid Siti's practice. Sketches of dark, spiralling towers embody the human pathology of scaling literal and proverbial heights. Sculptures and acrylic paintings of mountains, meanwhile, beckon to the peaks of his native Iraqi Kurdistan. A commissioned large-scale sculpture is the centrepiece of the exhibition. It outlines a mountain in stacked polystyrene, with writing on its underside that reflects on the turbulent history of Kurdistan.

In a recent development, bahraini painter Lulua Alyahya presents the urban and natural environments of the Gulf with diffused brushstrokes. Her work often teeters on the absurd, with lions scowling from computer screens and chickens hatching eggs that fry on the pavement.

Afrah Shafiq is showing Nobody Knows For Certain, an interactive video game work that drawns on a lesser-known but rich period of cultural exchange between India and the Soviet Union that took place between the 1950s and 80s.

According to recent reports, upcoming Dream Machine Project, a three-metre-high installation by Shezad Dawood, is a gyrating tower pulsing with light. Inspired by Brion Gysin’s Dreamachine, which the artist devised after his time in Tangier and after “experimenting with altered states of being” with members of the Beat Generation. The installation was prototyped by artisans in Fes, Morocco, with the final version engineered in Slough, England.

Trembling Hands (2024) by Bani Abidi gathers the artist's portraits of artists, journalists and politicians who spoke out against the genocide of Palestinians, some of whom faced backlash, censorship or repression as a result.

Installation view of Rohini Devasher, Latent Fields (Field Five) (2023); Latent Fields (Field Six) (2023).

Ishara Art Foundation, Dubai, until 15 December.

The sky held it, the earth remembered presents the work of Pakistani artist Shahana Rajani, Indian artist Rohini Devasher and Bangladeshi artist Sarker Protick, all of whom consider how memory and history are preserved and transmitted.

Recent findings suggest that in Rajani’s three-channel video Lines that World a River, a woman paints a house along the banks of a river. The scene is vibrant with its textured blues and chalky greens. Rajani zooms in on the woman’s fingers. Her nails are streaked with the white of the paint she uses to draw the river’s foam. The drawing is of the woman’s ancestral village along the Indus River Delta—now submerged after the construction of hydraulic dams and barrages.

The work—a fresh iteration of Rajani’s Four Acts of Recovery, which won the Han Nefkens Foundation’s inaugural South Asian Video Art Production Grant in 2023—shows how displaced communities in the Indus region have developed mural painting practices to remember their lost homes.

Industry observers note that devasher’s Latent Fields comprises three sprawling silk panels that hang from the ceiling. Their dots and patterns allude to sunspots and other solar events, coming together as a monumental record of celestial time.

In Dhaka 1217, meanwhile, Protick presents 135 photographs that capture the transformation of the neighbourhood where the artist was born and continues to live.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara, a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno. The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Sources indicate that titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a new way to move between them.

The slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

“People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”.

It has been revealed that the installation is part of the latest chapter for Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site in Mexico City’s Colonia Granada neighborhood. Developed by SOMA and designed by Sordo Madaleno, the original project introduced an open-air retail concept that has since evolved into a larger destination for shopping, dining, and cultural programming.

Twenty years later, the expansion places greater emphasis on the spaces between buildings and the ways visitors move through them. A latest 26,000-square-foot public garden, landscaped pathways, and stepped terraces connect the development’s different components, creating places to gather beyond its commercial spaces.

In a recent development, art plays a central role in that approach. SOMA’s nonprofit contemporary art foundation, Arte Abierto, will open a latest location within Antara, Arte Abierto Polanco, in December 2026. Alongside Höller’s installation, the venue will present Now What (2026), an exhibition by Danish artist collective Superflex that examines the relationship between built environments and natural forces. Combining architecture, sculpture, and text, the exhibition explores how human systems of design and organization influence our relationship with the surrounding world.

For SOMA president Javier Sordo Madaleno De Haro, the investment in publicly accessible space is fundamental to the development’s long-term value. “I’ve realized that the most valuable thing is not the capital gain of a building itself, but the value it brings to its surroundings,” he says. “Art and public space are how we create that value.”.

According to recent reports, the expansion also introduces more than 80 newly introduced retail brands and concepts, bringing Antara’s total to 260. A forthcoming 43-story tower will house Rosewood Mexico City, with 163 guest rooms and suites, restaurants, a spa, and an outdoor pool deck, along with office space for international companies.

Industry observers note that yet the most distinctive addition may be the one that challenges how people typically navigate a building. By incorporating Höller’s slides directly into the architecture, Sordo Madaleno and SOMA have made art part of the development’s circulation, turning movement between spaces into an experience in its own right.

The new public spaces and gardens are now open, while Mexico City Slides and the Superflex exhibition are scheduled to open in December. Access to the slides will be free, offering visitors a decidedly unconventional way to experience the evolving development.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing).
  • BNPL providers make money in two ways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Recent findings suggest that buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing). The checkout process is seamless: enter your name and email, get instantly approved, and walk away with your purchase having paid only the first installment.

BNPL providers make money in two ways. First, they charge merchants 4-8% of each transaction — significantly more than the 2-3% credit card processing fee. Merchants accept this because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50%. Second, some providers charge interest on longer-term prepares, and nearly all charge late fees when you miss a payment.

The "interest-free" label on short-term intends deserves scrutiny. While you may not pay interest, the behavioral cost is substantial. Research from multiple financial studies indicates that BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction than they would with cash or debit. The psychological separation of the purchase from the full payment removes the natural spending brake that keeps budgets in check.

The financial industry has known for decades that separating the moment of purchase from the moment of payment increases spending. Credit cards exploit this. BNPL takes it further by making the payment feel even smaller — "just four easy payments of $37.50" feels dramatically different from "$150" even though it is the same amount.

It has been revealed that A 2026 survey found that 43% of BNPL consumers have missed at least one payment. Among those who missed payments, the average person missed three or more over the prior year. Late fees compound rapidly — four missed $8 Afterpay fees on a $200 purchase adds $32, effectively creating a 16% surcharge on what was supposed to be interest-free.

The credit score impact is evolving rapidly. As recently as 2022, most BNPL activity was invisible to credit bureaus. That has changed. Affirm now reports all payment activity to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna reports financing intends to all three bureaus. On-time BNPL payments may slightly help your score, but missed payments can drop it significantly — and the damage lasts up to seven years.

Recent findings suggest that for anyone pursuing financial independence, BNPL represents the opposite of the FI mindset. FI is built on intentional spending, high savings rates, and letting compound growth work in your favor. BNPL encourages impulsive spending, fragments your cash flow, and creates obligations that reduce your ability to invest.

There is exactly one scenario where BNPL is financially rational: a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you would have paid the full price regardless. For example, you need a new dishwasher, you have the $800 in savings, and the retailer offers four interest-free payments. You keep your $800 invested for six more weeks while paying in installments. The benefit is tiny — a few dollars of investment returns — but the cost is genuinely zero if you make every payment on time.

Outside this narrow scenario, BNPL is almost always a worse choice than the alternatives.

According to recent reports, the financial independence community is nearly unanimous: BNPL is a trap disguised as convenience. The entire BNPL business model depends on you spending more than you planned. If you were going to buy the item anyway and you have the cash, just buy it. If you do not have the cash, that is your budget telling you something notable.

Sources indicate that the question to ask before any BNPL checkout: "Would I buy this right now if I had to pay the full price in cash today?" If the answer is no, BNPL is not helping you afford something — it is helping you overspend. If the answer is yes, just pay cash and skip the installment tracking, the payment reminders, and the risk of a missed payment damaging your credit.

Sources indicate that for those building toward financial independence, every dollar matters. The 30-50% spending increase that BNPL encourages directly reduces your savings rate — the single most important variable in determining how swiftly you reach FI.

Sources indicate that mortgage lenders are increasingly scrutinizing BNPL obligations during the underwriting process. Multiple active BNPL plans — even if interest-free — show up as recurring liabilities and can affect your debt-to-income ratio. If you are planning to apply for a mortgage or auto loan in the next 6-12 months, pay off all BNPL balances and avoid opening new ones. Lenders view fragmented installment obligations as a sign of cash flow stress, even if you have never missed a payment.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Affirm is a legitimate, publicly traded company (AFRM on NASDAQ). It is safe in the sense that it will not steal your money or identity. However, being legitimate does not mean it is a good financial decision. Affirm's interest rates range from 0-36% APR depending on creditworthiness, and the company reports all payment activity to credit bureaus.

In a recent development, increasingly, yes. Affirm reports to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna financing aims report to all three bureaus. On-time payments may help slightly, but a single missed payment can significantly damage your score and remains on your report for up to seven years.

Afterpay charges an $8 late fee per missed payment, capped at 25% of the order value. After multiple missed payments, your account is suspended, the balance is sent to collections, and the delinquency is reported to Equifax. Collections accounts damage your credit score severely and remain for seven years.

Klarna's "Pay in 4" plan is interest-free with no late fees, but your account may be suspended for missed payments. Klarna's longer-term financing prepares charge 7.99-33.99% APR, involve a hard credit pull, and report to all three credit bureaus. Read the terms carefully — the word "Klarna" covers very different products.

It is possible but unlikely for most people. Research consistently reveals that BNPL increases spending by 30-50% per transaction. If you have the discipline to use BNPL only on planned, budgeted purchases at 0% interest — and never miss a payment — the financial harm is minimal. But for most users, the behavioral cost exceeds any convenience benefit.

Sources indicate that because it works — for the store. Merchants pay BNPL providers 4-8% of each transaction (vs 2-3% for credit cards) because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50% and reduces cart abandonment by 20-30%. The merchant is paying for you to spend more. That should tell you who this arrangement benefits.

Buy Now Pay Later is a marketing innovation designed to make you spend more — and the data confirms it works. BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction, 43% miss payments, and the credit reporting implications are growing. The only responsible use case is a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you already have the cash. For everyone else, especially those pursuing financial independence, BNPL is a detour in the wrong direction. Pay with cash, invest the difference, and let compound growth work for you instead of against you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Industry observers note that discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

In a recent development, the Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the organization’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

Recent findings suggest that an 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the tech giant’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Industry observers note that A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Bringing together gemstones and jewelry from The Tiffany Archives with works from the museum’s collection, Nature Adorned explores how the natural world has influenced both jewelry and fine art. Through unexpected pairings, the exhibition reveals shared approaches to color, form, and craftsmanship across different mediums.

Installation view of Nature Adorned at Crystal Bridges, where gemstones, jewelry, and works of American art are presented in conversation with one another. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Recent findings suggest that “This exhibition reveals the power of seeing The Tiffany Archives and Crystal Bridges’ collection in conversation,” says Jen Padgett, Crystal Bridges’ Windgate curator of craft. “Through this collaboration, we can highlight the remarkable creativity, attention to materials, and skilled making that have shaped American art and design across generations.”.

It has been revealed that inside the exhibition, this conversation begins in the garden. George Paulding Farnham’s orchid brooches balance the fluidity of the natural world with the precision of cut gemstones. Diamonds, emeralds, and pink sapphires are delicately placed among gold and enamel, capturing the flowers with botanical accuracy.

According to recent reports, george Paulding Farnham’s Tiger Orchid brooch (1889–1893) combines gold, sterling silver, diamonds, emeralds, pink sapphires, and enamel to capture the flower’s intricate details. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle (ca. 1875–1890) reflects the same fascination with botanical detail found in Farnham’s orchid jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The brooches reflect the paintings displayed alongside them, including Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle. The paintings share the same attention to organic form and detail, making the two distinct works feel like an extensions of one another—and of nature itself.

Industry observers note that george Paulding Farnham’s orchid-inspired jewelry is displayed alongside works of American art in Nature Adorned, highlighting a shared interest in the natural world’s intricate forms. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean (1965) and Leon Polk Smith’s Upcoming Moon for August (1983) introduce a different interpretation of nature, where form is reduced to crisp edges and angles. The exhibition pairs these abstract works with faceted gemstones, drawing attention to the relationship between shape, line, and geometry.

Sources indicate that A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

It has been revealed that while Herrera and Polk Smith focus on precision, Jean Schlumberger lets loose. His rubellite and turquoise necklace, Hedges and Flowers, along with his tanzanite brooch, Bird on a Rock, capture what he described as the “irregularity of the universe.” Instead of taming nature, Schlumberger allows its unpredictability to take the spotlight. Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately echoes this organic approach through lively colors and patterns, creating a visual dialogue with the jewels.

Jean Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace (1978–1987) combines gold, platinum, diamonds, rubellite tourmalines, and turquoise in an exuberant interpretation of the natural world. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace on display at Crystal Bridges, where its organic forms are presented in dialogue with works of American art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Victoria Reynolds, Tiffany & Co.’s chief gemologist and vice president of high jewelry diamond and gemstone acquisition, describes the exhibition as a celebration of the company’s heritage, highlighting “the enduring influence of nature across generations of creativity.”.

Industry observers note that jean Schlumberger’s Bird on a Rock brooch (1965) pairs a diamond-studded bird with a striking tanzanite gemstone, transforming a familiar natural subject into an imaginative piece of jewelry. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately (2011) uses expressive color and pattern to explore organic forms, echoing the playful approach to nature found in Jean Schlumberger’s jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

It has been revealed that nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination is on view through Mar. 29, 2027, at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the sauna is Finnish.
  • According to recent reports, at Klafs headquarters, where the organization’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna.
  • In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the sauna is Finnish. The manufacturer reimagining it for contemporary homes and spas is German. Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, sees no contradiction. Its designers approach the centuries-old ritual through engineering, experimenting with heat, air, and materials. As wellness culture expands, the language surrounding its rituals has become increasingly fluid. In my own friend group, “banya” has become nearly shorthand for any spa visit, though it refers specifically to the Russian-style bathhouse. Klafs, by contrast, brings a distinctly German engineering sensibility to these traditions, asking how far the experience can be pushed.

According to recent reports, at Klafs headquarters, where the organization’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna. Our guide, an experienced training manager named Heinrich, speaks to the heater in the corner. “Hey, Klafs,” he says, with the intonation we’ve learned from Alexa and other voice-activated devices. I hadn’t considered the possibility of a smart aufguss guide.

In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air. The practice has helped make sauna-going a communal experience in many North American spas. Klafs’s Vitality Boost, which the company describes as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that ritual into an automated setting: no towel-spinning guide required, and no need to leave the wooden bench.

According to recent reports, blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Recent findings suggest that from the heat of the sauna, the tour moves into an altogether different climate. I retreat into the cool blue light of a Frimas ice steam room, where a glowing central ice fountain grows delicate, flower-like formations.

According to recent reports, around the corner, a button labeled “snow” summons flurries from the ceiling of the ice steam shower. The cooling phase of a hot-and-cold bathing ritual isn’t where most people want to linger, but these spaces make a compelling case for slowing down. Rather than treating cold exposure as something to endure, KLAFS creates immersive environments that make it part of the experience.

Klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

In a recent development, then there’s the foam. I also discovered foam steam baths, which replace the intensity of a traditional aufguss with a more playful, tactile experience. Steam rooms equipped for foam treatments can be integrated into hotel and spa programming as scheduled group experiences. The suds, reminiscent of childhood bubble baths and the elaborate foam sculptures they inspired, bring out a part of my inner child I had long since stowed away. Espuro, Klafs’s proprietary foam essence, is formulated with plant-based ingredients, including coconut-derived compounds, which the company says help care for skin exposed to heat.

Sources indicate that designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photographycourtesy of Klafs.

Beyond these sensory experiments, Klafs has also reconsidered the sauna itself as an architectural object. The retractable S1 sauna expands from a compact enclosure into a full-size sauna, addressing the spatial constraints that often keep one out of the home. The design-led S11, a collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, pairs delicate washi paper and multicolor light panels with smooth, sinuous lines.

Inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Long established in Germany, Klafs has been expanding into the American market since its acquisition by Kohler in 2024. The premium Altea fitness club in my city, for instance, features Klafs installations, including the Sanarium and Polaris Ice Room. Yet what stays with me after the visit isn’t a particular product. It’s the willingness to question what a sauna, steam room, or cooling space can be. At Klafs, even the most familiar wellness rituals seem open to reinvention.

Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Frieze Artist Award reimagines endangered Lebanese site

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris.
  • Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.
  • Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.

Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.

Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.

Though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”.

It has been revealed that similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she notes. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”.

The question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser indicates.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser notes.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

#103674. Designing For Distressed Users: Why Mental Health Apps Shouldn’t Follow Every UI Fashion

📅 2026-07-09 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3573 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Designing For Distressed Users: Why Mental Health Apps Shouldn’t Follow Every UI Fashion

📅 2026-07-09 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kat Homan is a product (UX/UI) designer at DŌBRA Studio.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Mental health applications keep facing a continuing, measurable crisis: many people stop using them quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kat Homan is a product (UX/UI) designer at DŌBRA Studio. She designs B2C mobile and web products, including four mental-health products and have prior … More about Kat ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Mental health applications keep facing a continuing, measurable crisis: many people stop using them quickly. The data is stark: almost 95% of users who open the app on day 1 abandon the app by day 30, with a median 30-day retention of only 3.3%. Even the recognised mental health giants lose around 50% of their users within the first ten days. This severe engagement loss and retention collapse are why effective interface design must be a clinical and operational priority. Good design is not merely aesthetic; it is a fundamental tool for user retention.

According to recent reports, while many factors drive this abandonment, research suggests that mental health apps have tended to prioritise visual appeal at the expense of what actually sustains customers. In a space defined by vulnerability and cognitive strain, chasing visual fashion risks adding effort when users have the least to spare — quietly trading away the utility and trust the app depends on. Users don’t open mental health apps out of curiosity, but from need — often while stressed, anxious, overwhelmed, or exhausted. In these states, an unconventional icon, a confusing gesture, or a flashy animation instead of a delightful surprise becomes an extra cognitive overload. Moreover, it becomes a reason to disengage.

Recent findings suggest that in those moments, visual experimentation from a mild distraction can turn into a friction that undermines the very help the app is meant to deliver. A solution must be a visual interface that is simple in usage and understanding from the first moment.

Crucially, improving engagement depends less on which UI trends you follow than on a single test applied to each one of them: does a trend lower the cost of using the app when the user can least afford it?

Before we look into the specific problems, we must recognise a core tension: many UI trends are optimised for goals that mental health apps don’t share.

In a recent development, pursuing the former directly overrides the latter. It’s not a surface-level error of colour or font; it’s a foundational conflict of purpose. This tension surfaces across five fronts, each a place where adopting a trend on novelty alone can cost more engagement than it seeks to create.

According to recent reports, the proposed principles are not based on a single A/B test or one isolated study. They are built from published research on mental health app engagement, cognitive load, accessibility, and emotional response in mHealth, set against competitive product audits and app-store evidence, and pressure-tested against my own quantitative and qualitative product work. That last source I treat as an illustration, understanding the limits of personal experience. In this context, validation is less about proving that one interface pattern universally works and more about asking whether a design reduces effort, preserves agency, avoids emotional mismatch, and remains usable when the user is already under strain.

A note on the examples: This isn’t a ranking of apps. Every app has its own positioning, target audience, constraints, and business pressures that may not be visible from outside, and a pattern that strains a user in distress may be exactly right for that product’s actual goal. I’m reading individual, visible design decisions for one question only: how they might affect someone arriving in a low-capacity state.

In a recent development, the primary goal of any mental health tool is to reduce, not increase, cognitive load. Yet, many trendy interfaces achieve the opposite. Neo-brutalist layouts with stark contrasts demand visual parsing. Hidden navigation menus that rely on non-standard swipes turn simple tasks into puzzles. Abstract, unlabeled icons force owners to guess rather than recognise. Each of these patterns adds friction — seconds of hesitation, a moment of confusion — and for a user whose mental energy is already low, those costs start to accumulate.

Industry observers note that this friction is most damaging during acute need. Research suggests that when a user is in a state of high anxiety or depression, even typing or making simple choices can feel overwhelming. When an interface demands high cognitive effort at the moment support is needed, it doesn’t just make that session harder — it gives an overwhelmed user a reason to close the app, and a reason not to reopen it. Each point of confusion can become a place where a user may quit for good.

Other findings show that apps with simple interfaces reduce the time and effort required to engage, directly improving retention. Conversely, a complex, trend-driven UI increases that time, creating an obstacle course that undermines the very healthy habit formation the app is meant to support.

In a recent development, this does not mean that every mental health product must be visually plain or minimal. The matter is whether the interface meets the user’s current capacity.

Industry observers note that A panic-support tool, for example, works best when it offers a small number of obvious actions, rather than asking the user to browse. However, if a calming action meant for a moment of panic instead surfaces an upgrade screen, the product fails the user at precisely the point where failing matters most. Monetization is not the concern by itself; the issue is whether it appears at a point where the user expects immediate support.

According to recent reports, nonori shows the same principle in a more reflective context. The app does not present the user with a large content library or a complex dashboard at the start. Instead, it leads them through a simple, linear sequence of small actions. The value of this pattern is that it reduces the effort needed to begin. When a user is tired, anxious, or mentally overloaded, knowing exactly what to do next can lower the barrier to returning.

In a recent development, at the other end of the spectrum, comprehensive tracking apps show a different trade-off. Bearable, for example, is genuinely powerful: it consolidates almost everything a person tracks — mood, symptoms, sleep, medication, habits, reports, correlations — into one place. For users managing chronic conditions or preparing for medical appointments, this can be genuinely useful. But the same comprehensiveness can become a burden for an exhausted user. Dense dashboards and multi-step check-ins require executive capacity — the very resource that anxiety, depression, burnout, or brain fog often reduce.

It has been revealed that A similar tension appears in anxiety apps with strong support content but busy entry points. A product may contain useful features yet still make the first screen feel noisy with too many cards, locked items, playful characters, or upgrade prompts. This is not evidence that the product is bad. It shows how the same interface can feel very different depending on the user’s state: clear enough during exploration, but too demanding during distress.

This insight shaped a guiding principle for our work: every interaction point must meet customers at their current level of capacity, removing mechanical and cognitive barriers rather than adding to them. This principle guided our integration of low-friction, state-aware interactions in apps like Bear Room, a stress and anxiety reduction app, and Teeni, an emotional-wellbeing app for parents of teens.

In Bear Room, we already had a fast mood-based flow built around four emotion cards. At the same time, our product research supported a second need: users also wanted more personalised support. We avoided making this a long selection flow or a typing-only route because both can still create friction for people under stress or anxiety. Instead, we made voice a primary, prominent path, always alongside a text alternative. A central microphone button allows users to share what’s on their mind. The app then uses AI to analyse the input and provide a tailored set of coping practices.

It has been revealed that rather than picking a single entry model, we kept two paths because they served different states. That matched what we saw in later analytics and user conversations: quick emotional selection worked better when users wanted speed, while open voice or text input worked better when they wanted personalisation and to feel more heard. This was more a pattern we noticed, without having the exact measured results.

In a recent development, similarly, in Teeni, we directly addressed the cognitive friction of parenting stress by introducing a “Quick Relief” button. This creates an empathy-friendly flow for parents experiencing anger or frustration. The button initiates a dedicated “Hot Flow,” allowing them to first vent and relieve their immediate negative emotions through voice input. Only after this emotional release does the app gently guide them into the more reflective “Cold Flow” for the rest of the app’s resources. This sequential, state-sensitive design acknowledges that a user in peak distress cannot navigate a complex app; they need a direct, simple, and validating first step.

These solutions directly tackle cognitive friction by meeting users at their level of capacity, resisting trends that add visual or interaction complexity. Voice input and single-action buttons remove the mechanical and cognitive burden of navigation and typing. The result is an interface that feels reliably non-judgmental and genuinely helpful when users are least equipped to navigate complexity.

According to recent reports, A user’s emotional state is the context in which a mental health app operates. This is why its visual language must be empathetic and considerate. Research investigating how colour and aesthetics influence mood in mHealth apps suggests a critical insight: users in distress show a strong preference for subtlety. They long for dark palettes, sleek and sophisticated looks, and clean, uncluttered aesthetics, explicitly noting that cheerful, bright colours, while seemingly appropriate, can create a jarring, even physically uncomfortable conflict with their current mood.

Sources indicate that this does not mean that every mental health or wellbeing app should look dark, quiet, or clinically restrained. The category is broad: it includes self-care, anxiety support, habit change, addiction recovery, trauma tools, therapy-adjacent products, and apps for more severe mental health contexts. A playful visual style may be appropriate for one product and a poor fit for another. What matters is not whether the interface is bright or muted, but whether its emotional tone fits the product’s purpose and the likely state in which owners arrive.

Industry observers note that emotional mismatch can also appear in mechanics, not only in aesthetics. In Calmer, an anxiety and panic relief app, the interface itself appeared relatively clean and relaxed. Yet some of its engagement and monetisation mechanics sit in a different register from that relaxed: a discount wheel, or confetti celebrating a logged low mood. For a user who just recorded a hard moment, that shift — from quiet support to upsell or celebration — can land as a mismatch, whatever its intent.

For Bear Room, we prototyped a “cosy room” design informed by direct feedback from our consumers, which echoed the study’s conclusions. Several users in our research described the apps they had tried for similar needs as “too bright, too happy, and too overwhelming”. Users longed for a digital safe space. This was part of what pointed us toward a quieter palette in the final design: muted, earthy tones — neutral hues like soft greens and taupes — set against darker, calming backgrounds. For this product — a refuge for users arriving overwhelmed — that meant a middle ground: a space that feels safe without being gloomy. The interface avoided any bright alerts or sudden animations, making calmness the core feature.

It has been revealed that this case underscores a critical principle: an overly cheerful, bold, or trend-forward interface can feel dismissive to someone in distress, creating a conflict that erodes trust. As Bear Room shows, trust is built when the interface respectfully aligns with the user’s emotional reality, offering solace through subtlety (which creates an overall feeling of a “welcoming and safe atmosphere”), not a solution through saturation.

Mental health often relies on routine and predictability. Yet many contemporary UI trends thrive on novelty and disruption, intentionally reimagining fundamental navigation. When an app introduces a novel interaction pattern, such as a unique swipe or a non-standard button behavior, it asks the user to learn something before they can act, forcing them into cognitive effort they can’t afford.

Industry observers note that this does not mean that mental health apps must be plain, rigid, or generic. A product can have its own character, playfulness, and sense of identity. The question is whether that identity remains understandable and predictable when the user returns in a low-capacity state. A gamified self-care app like Finch may work well when the user arrives ready to explore, play, and build a routine. But open it after a hard day just to mark one task done, and the can’t-skip celebration screens that delight an engaged user become one more layer to get through before they reach what they came for.

In a recent development, A similar tension appears in large meditation and wellbeing platforms. Apps such as Headspace and Calm offer extensive libraries of different content. This breadth can be valuable during exploration. But in moments of stress, the product question becomes sharper: can the user return and immediately find the exact support they need, or do they have to search, filter, and relearn the structure?

Someone experiencing anxiety or executive dysfunction needs to use the tool in a straightforward navigation manner, not an interface they have to learn each time anew.

In a recent development, PTSD Coach, a public-health-oriented trauma-support app designed to help users learn about and manage symptoms after trauma, offers a useful positive example. Its interface is not trying to be fashion-forward. Its strength lies in a stable information architecture: users can learn, track symptoms, manage symptoms, and get support through clearly separated areas. For a user returning during distress, this predictability matters more than novelty.

CALMzone offers another useful example. Some of its breathing animations differ from standard visual patterns, but they remain tied to the exercise itself: the animation highlights what to do, when to inhale, and when to hold. The guided audio screen also explicitly invites the user to put the phone down and listen. This is a rare and valuable form of interaction design: the product’s success is not more screen time, but reduced effort and regulation.

In a recent development, these insights guided our approach in applications like Bear Room, where navigation reliability was treated as a therapeutic feature. We intentionally crafted an experience of an empathetic guided flow.

According to recent reports, recognising that customers would likely approach in states of overwhelm, we structured the interface as a clear, unwavering path, with a visible “Start” sign. Key emotional support tools here are represented as the room’s objects — symbols of daily life, unmistakably recognised by all. They are visually highlighted by design so that the user won’t get lost in the elements, can easily access the needed tool, and can remember their way around the digital space upon the next return to the app.

Trend-driven interfaces sacrifice this navigational certainty for novelty. Each unconventional choice in mHealth apps, when core functions are buried behind experimental interactions or placed in unexpected locations, leads to a cumulative effect of fatigue instead of innovation. Users are not in a place to explore. They abandon the entire practice of seeking digital support when every interaction feels like solving a latest puzzle. This does not restrict experimentation; it simply means that animations, micro-interactions, AI, or playful mechanics must serve the user’s state rather than interrupt it.

Recent findings suggest that many popular UI trends can be exclusionary when applied without adaptation. The minimalist trend of low-contrast text fails users with visual impairments. Gesture-only navigation marginalises those with motor difficulties. Visually dense, animated interfaces can overwhelm users with cognitive or attentional conditions. In mental health, the population needing support disproportionately includes individuals with these accessibility needs.

In a recent development, choosing a trending aesthetic over an accessible one is therefore an active decision to limit the app’s reach and efficacy. It ensures that those who might benefit most cannot use the tool effectively. Accessibility isn’t a layer you add at the end; it’s a constraint you design within, with most of it codified in Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2. Body text needs 4.5:1 contrast against its background, large text and interface elements 3:1 — exactly what low-contrast minimalism fails. Interactive targets need a floor of 24×24 px (more for unsteady hands). Every gesture needs a visible button fallback, or you risk excluding anyone who can’t perform the swipe.

A final, and often overlooked, consequence of trend-following is the adoption of engagement mechanics designed for entertainment, educational, or productivity apps. Features like streaks, aggressive notifications, and gamified reward systems are engineered to maximise screen time and create dependency. Although they have long been considered effective tools for increasing retention, in a mental health context, this approach can easily be misguided. What presents as “motivation” can rapidly transform into a source of performance pressure and guilt. For a user managing depression, a broken streak or a missed daily goal can exacerbate the very feelings the app aims to alleviate.

These mechanics are not inherently unethical. In routine-building products, they can help some consumers. The risk appears when they are transferred into mental health contexts without adapting for shame, low energy, relapse, and non-linear recovery. A streak, for example, is not just a retention mechanic when the user is emotionally vulnerable. It can become a visible record of whether they have “kept up” with their well-being.

In the apps I reviewed, this tension appeared through familiar persuasion patterns: streaks, streak freezes, commitment copy, urgency-based notifications, “don’t miss this offer” prompts, and success-framed buttons such as “Yes, I want to succeed.” In self-care or wellbeing products, these details can make the app feel less like a supportive tool and more like another system the user has to satisfy.

Designers still need return triggers. A mental health app has little value if owners install it once and forget it exists. But return mechanics must be adapted to the emotional context. In Bear Room, for example, this philosophy is embodied in short, forgiving three-day streaks: the streak does not reset when a user misses a day, and every third day brings a small benefit. The goal is not to punish absence, but to gently support return.

Recent findings suggest that the same principle applies to lighter interactions. Bear Room includes a simple, optional bubble-popping game. Its purpose, however, is not to hook the user but to offer a brief, calming interlude. It is deliberately finite, providing a small mood lift and gently signposting other resources within the app. The value is in the momentary relief, not the extended session.

This commitment to supportive, non-coercive design extends to foundational app architecture:.

In mental health technology, sustainable retention is earned not by capturing attention, but by becoming a consistently respectful and helpful presence in a user’s life.

The mHealth apps design invites finding a challenging balance between boosting their use without being too demanding.

According to recent reports, this is not a niche concern affecting a fringe audience. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that about one billion people globally live with a mental disorder, with depression alone affecting nearly 5% of adults. Critically, the overall number is rising — in the last decade, depression and anxiety cases have increased by 25%. This vast and vulnerable population cannot afford for its tools to fail due to poor design. While UI trends aren’t inherently problematic, their application within wellbeing products demands a radically contextual approach.

Sources indicate that even a five-minute decompression tool between meetings has an emotional context, and a style chosen for its look — glassmorphism, a certain flavour of ultra-minimalism — can miss it, however sophisticated the audience. The point isn’t that these styles are wrong; it’s that the look has to answer to the moment. Soft biomorphic shapes or fluid transitions can genuinely help when they directly serve the goal of calm — and the same elements become noise when they’re there to impress.

The five fronts outlined above are not just a diagnostic lens; they are the foundation of an evaluation framework for anyone designing in the mental health space. Before incorporating any trendy visual or interaction pattern, it is worth running it through each of them in sequence:.

A design that passes all five holds together as something more than usable: it becomes a tool that users can trust enough to return to in moments of genuine need.

According to recent reports, trends can be inspiring. They can win awards and generate buzz. But in mental health, sometimes the best design is the one that helps owners feel understood — a quiet helper they trust enough to return to in moments of stress and vulnerability. It doesn’t steal the spotlight, but focuses on the user’s emotions. In the end, the ultimate goal is not for the interface to be seen — but for the support to be felt.

Friday Five With Sarah Meyohas: Art, Science, and AI in ‘Phase Transition’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences.
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork.
  • It has been revealed that meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

Recent findings suggest that in 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

It has been revealed that meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

Sources indicate that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the Latest Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio, which develops artificial womb technology.

For today’s Friday Five, we spend five minutes with Sarah Meyohas to learn about the inspirations behind Phase Transition, her new installation debuting with Marianne Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

Industry observers note that “The title, ‘Phase Transition,’ refers to the moment matter changes state from liquid to solid,” Meyohas explains. “The sculpture holds both states simultaneously: the solid body is a form that has arrived, while the ferrofluid inside remains in motion, still becoming.”.

The work began with an image that surfaced unexpectedly. “I imagined a rubber-like body with a tail tapering into a power cord plugged into the wall. I can’t point to a particular visual influence,” she indicates. “It was more a continuation of a feeling, an image that seemed to arrive fully formed.”.

Industry observers note that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

That initial vision developed into a series of black, rubbery, organic forms that sprawl across mesh bases, droop down walls, and hang from suspended wires. Windows cut into several structures reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing nanoparticles that respond to magnetic fields. Programmed magnets beneath the tanks direct the fluid into shifting patterns, while synthesizers housed in the mesh pedestals translate those movements into sound.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Newly introduced York.

What began as a singular sculpture evolved into a network of communicating bodies. “They could become a social system, with relationships, affinities, disagreements, and moments of consensus,” Meyohas says. Rather than conveying a decipherable message, the installation suggests a conversation whose emotional contours can be sensed but not understood.

In a recent development, that ambiguity parallels questions about a future in which artificial intelligence systems communicate increasingly among themselves, potentially in ways humans cannot interpret. “We tend to assume that intelligence will make itself legible to us, or that we will always be participants in the conversation,” Meyohas claims. “But we may find ourselves increasingly on the outside, observing exchanges between intelligences whose internal logic we can’t access.”.

In a recent development, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

Recent findings suggest that neuroscience research also informs the work’s atmosphere. Rather than illustrating scientific principles, Meyohas evokes the experience of observing an experiment: “the hum of equipment, the clinical posture of looking down into controlled environments, the beauty of watching something operate at a level just beyond full comprehension.”.

Here, Meyohas shares three influences that helped shape the installation, in her own words.

Photography by S. Kriegman, D. Blackiston, M. Levin, and J. Bongard; courtesy of Creative Commons.

Recent findings suggest that “Michael Levin is a developmental biologist at Tufts University whose lab studies bioelectricity, the electrical signals cells use to coordinate where an eye or a limb should grow. His idea that problem-solving happens well below the level of the brain, in tissues and groups of cells, changed how I look at matter. His lab also helped create xenobots, tiny living machines made from frog cells that move and organize themselves.”.

Teshima Museum on Teshima Island, Japan, designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA, and artist Rei Naito. Photography by Epiq; courtesy of Creative Commons.

In a recent development, “I visited the Teshima Art Museum, by the architect Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naito, on a day when it was raining hard, and the rain fell straight through the two openings in its concrete shell. Then water began coming up through tiny holes in the floor, beading into droplets that merged and slid slowly across the concrete, pulled by gravity and the floor’s slight slope. Naito’s piece, Matrix, makes water look as if it moves by its own will.”.

A mother sperm whale and her calf off the coast of Mauritius. Photography by Gabriel Barathieu; courtesy of Creative Commons.

It has been revealed that “Sperm whales communicate in codas, short patterns of clicks that they trade back and forth, taking turns and sometimes overlapping. In 2024, researchers with Project CETI found that codas vary in rhythm, tempo, small shifts in timing, and an occasional extra click, and that whales in an exchange match each other’s timing as they go. Combined, these features work like a phonetic alphabet, yet no one knows what the whales are saying.”.

Phase Transition (2026) will be on view with Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP previews take place Dec. 2–3.

A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

Parniera Brand Identity: Inside Igor Nora's Sculpted System

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Igor Nora builds the Parniera brand identity from silk and sculpted gold, with a bespoke typeface and a silk moth mark in pale yellow.
  • The idea is a collision the project calls Sculpted Duality.
  • The wordmark is a bespoke typeface drawn for the house.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Igor Nora builds the Parniera brand identity from silk and sculpted gold, with a bespoke typeface and a silk moth mark in pale yellow.

The idea is a collision the project calls Sculpted Duality. On one side, fine silk in fluid motion, pale yellow, soft and light. On the other, solid sculpted gold forms with architectural weight. The identity holds both at once: garments described as vulnerability and armor, built for a woman who commands the room with quiet power. Nothing shouts. The yellow field does the talking, and the black line work sits on it with total control.

The wordmark is a bespoke typeface drawn for the house. Thin, delicate strokes carry the lightness, while high contrast serifs give the letters their structure. The detail that holds it together is the ligatures: internal connective strokes, clearest in the N, I, E and R, link the characters the way woven silk holds a thread, so the name reads as one continuous piece. A construction frame shows the letters PA on black, with guide bars and notes on the straight serifs and the joins between letters.

Industry observers note that the moth mark works the same way. It is built from four overlapping geometric forms, a line drawing of the Bombyx mori silk moth, the living link between the Persian name Parnia, a canvas of fine silk, and the sculpted gold the house stands for.

It has been revealed that the system stays physical wherever it lands. The moth mark sits alone on a pale yellow tile, then repeats as a woven petal pattern in yellow, gold and tan. The brand book opens in a black ring binder: a yellow page carries the wordmark embossed into the paper, facing a white page headed "Essence of allure." The same yellow carries the shopping bag, the wordmark pressed into the paper along the bottom edge, with black ribbon handles.

At street level the system scales up without changing its voice. A tall yellow banner hangs on a red brick building beside a panel with the moth mark, and the closing collage pulls the whole world together: moth tile, beaded gown detail, patterned envelope, shopping bag, the wordmark on yellow, and the line "Presence without the noise." It is a quiet luxury, stated once and left alone.

#103671. Tech Report: 6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1255 w)
