Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

📅 2026-11-12 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

In a recent development, A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

According to recent reports, rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

According to recent reports, every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

An AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

We can call that the break-even line. Returns to owners come in three forms:.

It has been revealed that for example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool highlights the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

Sources indicate that four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

It has been revealed that these questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

Sources indicate that run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the concern alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

According to recent reports, count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

In a recent development, A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom claims to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

It has been revealed that you can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

Industry observers note that who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

It has been revealed that compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

For example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

The nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

In a recent development, every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

Error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

According to recent reports, automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, users stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

Sources indicate that map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

In a recent development, show customers where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

Sources indicate that letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

Recent findings suggest that still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

Research in radiology demonstrates how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result demonstrated how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

Recent findings suggest that question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

Industry observers note that ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

Table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

Sources indicate that put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

It has been revealed that let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

According to recent reports, question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

Question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

Question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

Industry observers note that on Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

Sources indicate that question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

According to recent reports, the feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

According to recent reports, two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

Everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that latest capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

Industry observers note that audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

Start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that people might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

The attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

According to recent reports, the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

It wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

The evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s Fresh York in May 1986 for $1m.

Gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Fresh York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

It has been revealed that A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s New York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s New York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

In a recent development, french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s Fresh York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Substantial name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

In a recent development, the monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively big price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

It has been revealed that picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

Recent findings suggest that the Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s Newly introduced York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

One of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, Latest Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article said the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

It hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s Fresh York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

It has been revealed that though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export concerns, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

According to recent reports, “It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” said Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

Lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

We asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most mentioned they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

According to recent reports, these results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

It has been revealed that this matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

According to recent reports, so how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

Here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge shows up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only demonstrates correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

And it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize concerns. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

Sources indicate that in other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

Industry observers note that not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

According to recent reports, pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

How many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

As AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding concerns, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing new gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

Sources indicate that found the glitch? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When issues end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

In a recent development, every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the issue comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

It has been revealed that A passing test shows a known matter hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

We’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

STUDIO HERRSTRÃM rebuilds the Milkshake brand identity around car culture, a redrawn splash mark, high-vis color and road signs.

Milkshake is a Stockholm label, a division of Sony Music Entertainment founded in 2019, and its latest identity starts in a car. The name was suggested on a car ride, milestones happened in cars, and new music was taken for a car test. The old splash is still there, redrawn as a rounded, blended symbol that reads like metal and liquid merging, and the wordmark runs through it with a zigzag cut that splits Milkshake into two stacked hits. On the posters the name fills the frame until the letters stop being text and start being the picture: acid yellow Milksh across the top, shake across the bottom.

The type system is Gates, a neo-grotesque from Contextype, shown in the specimen with arrows, asterisks, circled letters and roman numerals on a mauve field. The wordmark itself leans forward, its letters cut on a slant that matches the splash, and the supporting lockups borrow their logic from car window stickers and milk carton nutrition labels: small blocks of capitals that hold track names, release dates and the p-line symbol without breaking the grid.

The system proves itself on the objects it touches. A high-vis vest carries the full lockup on its back in black on acid yellow, with reflective bands borrowed from road markings. A neon green acrylic cube hangs outside the shopfront with the black wordmark on its face. A blender wears the whole icon set as stickers: the machine that makes the drink becomes the merch.

According to recent reports, color does the rest. Acid yellow is the signal color, while neon pink and soft lilac take the flavor cues and black keeps the contrast high. The same palette runs the subway poster for Tove Lo's single Me/You (always and forever), dated 18.09.26. Linn Wexell, founder and creative director of Milkshake, claims the creative work was smart and on point and the visuals stunning.

Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” states Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the new attribution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown. But not all Della Robbias were created equal. Scholars and collectors have long given strong preference to Luca della Robbia (1399/1400-1482), the founder of the dynasty, and his nephew Andrea della Robbia (1435-1525). Similar works by later Della Robbias and those produced by the workshop can come in a very distant third. For decades, Fresh York’s Frick Collection believed it owned a relief by the family workshop, dated no earlier than the 16th century. But now, after technical analysis and consultation with experts in the field, the museum has updated its Virgin and Child to a 15th-century original, likely from the 1470s or 80s.

“We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” states Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the new attribution.

Industry observers note that the framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs. Fashioned out of buff-coloured earthenware, it has the Della Robbia clan’s distinctive white and blue glazes, with, in this case, traces of gilding. The work was first acquired by Helen Clay Frick, Henry’s daughter, in 1922 and spent most of the last century stashed outside the main reading room of the Frick Art Research Library.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

Llanes Serrano indicates the road to the new attribution was filled with twists and turns, and an outright gap or two.

The early American luminary in Della Robbia studies was the Princeton University art historian Allan Marquand (1853-1924). Llanes Serrano states that in a 1906 publication Marquand identified the work, then in the possession of a private German collector, as being by either Luca or “very early Andrea”. Then, in 1914, he decided “that it had to be Andrea”. After it landed in the Frick family collection and found its way to the library entrance, it went from being a Della Robbia, generally, she says, to a work by Andrea—a decision, she notes, recorded by a librarian, though who actually made the decision is not known. Later, it was outright demoted to “school of Della Robbia” and has had that lower-rung status since at least 2008.

It has been revealed that julia Day, who was appointed last year as the Frick’s upcoming chief conservator, thought it was time to take a new look at the work after attending a Della Robbia conference in spring 2025. “I just thought that we have this piece, and nobody’s really spent time looking at it,” Day states.

Sources indicate that llanes Serrano, who analysed the relief over the last year in the Frick’s new conservation studio, states XRF analysisallowed her to move back the dating and place it closer to Andrea himself. “I took multiple readings on different spots on the back and front,” she says, of the non-invasive technique.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the frame of the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

According to recent reports, the process revealed the elements present in the glaze, and then she compared her results with other analyses of autograph Della Robbia works. This helped her to place it in the newly introduced 1470s-80s time frame, when the older Luca was giving way to the younger Andrea. Meanwhile, another clue was plainly visible: “The Christ Child is clothed,” she says. In later versions of the motif made by the sculptors and their workshop, she adds, it was more common to show him unclothed.

A few weeks ago, the museum moved the work away from the library, where it was out of view from the general public, and installed it in a damask-lined spot in the mansion’s first-floor Octagon Room, fresh from its makeover during the Frick’s recent renovation.

Day says this kind of conservation-guided upgrade is a rarity at the Frick, happening perhaps once a decade. The Virgin and Child is the only Della Robbia piece in the museum's collection, she adds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leonardo Pertileâs book design for ADI Design Museumâs Compasso dâOro packs 1,040 pages into twin cloth volumes set in OT Marmo.

In a recent development, compressing nearly seventy years of Italian industrial design into a 1,040-page brick isnât a subtle problem. Presented by Fondazione ADI, ADI Associazione per il Disegno Industriale, and ADI Design Museum, this Treccani monograph is edited by Beppe Finessi and designed by Leonardo Pertile as twin cloth editions. Brick-red cloth printed in royal blue marks the English Historical Collection with a yellow ribbon, while yellow cloth inked in red identifies the Italian Collezione Storica with a navy ribbon. Neither cover uses product photography. A large blind-debossed compass presses into the woven board under Omnitypeâs pre-release OT Marmo capitals, and opening the red cover flashes yellow endpaper beside three tall floor lamps.

According to the museumâs notes, the publication holds 2,275 images across three parts: ADI Design Museumâs archival role, the 1954â2022 Compasso dâOro Roll of Honour, and critical essays and interviews. Pertile keeps that scale legible by shifting the grid per section so the book design doesnât lose its rhythm. On pages 154 and 155, Anty Panseraâs essay wraps justified columns around four staggered black-and-white ceremony photos. Another spread runs a hand-drawn nebido logo study on millimeter graph paper across the top above justified prose and hanging-indent captions citing Franco Albini, Franca Helg, and Bob Noorda. Turn to pages 474 and 475 for Anno 1967 and the density jumps â Enzo Mariâs concentric Freud Opere sketches and Mario Piazzaâs ruled pull quote face Olivettiâs tight vertical matrix of color-coded marks.

Sources indicate that heavy catalogs donât work without quiet spreads. Page 577 pairs an overhead photo of a terracotta sofa and dark-green chaise directly above twin framed floor aims, leaving the plate clear of clutter. That open air widens in the essays and interviews. Alberto Saibeneâs Milano, 1954: cultura e industria opener floats OT Marmo headings high in white space above two narrow columns. On page 967, Beppe Finessiâs interview with Paola Antonelli switches to ragged-right text with outdented BF and PA initials in the margin so speakers scan fast. Itâs disciplined book design that makes a 1,040-page institutional archive easy to open and read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party. With Orbán’s culturally regressive movement in tatters, Budapest is now reclaiming its status as one of Europe’s most important artistic capitals, and experiencing a wave of visitors newly drawn to the city in the wake of the country’s political about-face.

Hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions. The sprawling, multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary, which once stretched from the Mediterranean to what is now southwestern Ukraine, rebelled against Hapsburg dominance in the mid-19th century. That break culminated in 1866, when Austria and Hungary became constituent parts of a new dual monarchy, spurring on the 1873 union of the separate towns of Buda and Pest, reconstituted as a Belle-Époque boomtown.

Hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility. The museum’s broad range of Old Master paintings and its world-class prints and drawings collection arguably make it the most important museum of its kind between Vienna and St. Petersburg. In 1957, the bulk of its Hungarian holdings were separated into a new institution, the Hungarian National Gallery, which eventually moved over to the Buda side of the city, into the onetime Habsburg Royal Palace. Though the Orbán regime had planned to rehouse it again, it remains in situ for the time being, and its collections of Hungarian art, spanning centuries, testifies to a rich and varied artistic tradition almost entirely unknown outside the country. Back over in Pest, a new cultural development, Müpa Budapest, opened in 2005, providing a home to the city’s Ludwig Museum, with a collection of contemporary art from national and international figures.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Recent findings suggest that raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508)Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareTiny and technically unfinished, with the Virgin’s face and the figures of the Christ child and St. John the Baptist mere underdrawings, this tempera-and-oil on panel work has a grace and graphic quality that have helped make it the best-known Renaissance work in the country.

Produced at the end of Raphael’s Florentine period, when his output still reflects a youthful interest in Leonard da Vinci, the painting apparently first made its way north of the Alps in the early 18th century during the papacy of Clement XI, landing in the Esterházy collection by 1812. Stolen in 1983, along with the museum’s prized Giorgione portrait and other works, it was recovered the following year in a Greek monastery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870).

Credit: Museum of Fine Arts Budapest – Hungarian National Gallery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870)Hungarian National GallerySzent György térIn Hungary’s heyday before the First World War, when Budapest began to compete with Vienna, painter Mihály Munkácsy was a national hero. Born in what is now Ukraine, then educated at the art academies of Vienna, Munich and Düsseldorf, he eventually settled in Paris, with a base of collectors stretching from Central Europe to the American Midwest. His Budapest funeral procession, in spring 1900, was witnessed by hundreds of thousands people and remains a unique event in the history of the country.

Industry observers note that working in a number of established genres, from history painting to portraiture, he went on to decorate both Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum and Budapest’s new Parliament building. But this breakthrough work—which scarcely gives a clue whether the condemned man in question is a criminal or a victim of injustice—remains his best known. Winning a gold medal at the 1870 Paris Salon, it was a main topic of conversation in the French capital during the final days of the doomed Second Empire.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareThe MFAB's prints and drawings collection has legendary status among scholars in the field, with key works stretching from Renaissance Italy to early 20th-century Vienna, leading up to the present day. This exquisite Leonardo drawing—one of three in the collection—is a preparatory work associated with a planned mural in Florence’s Palazzo Vecchio meant to commemorate the Florentine Republic’s victory over the Duchy of Milan in 1440.

Left unfinished in 1506, when Leonardo himself left for Milan, the partial mural, made using an unstable oil-based technique, was nonetheless one of Cinquecento Florence’s star attractions, until its degraded version fell victim to a 1560s renovation. This red-chalk drawing of a Florentine captain, produced using a live model, is known for its depiction of intense emotion.

Hungarian crown jewels on display in the parliament building.

Photo: Schopenhauer; Courtesy Wikimedia.

The Holy Crown of Hungary (around 12th century)Hungarian ParliamentKossuth Lajos térThe Kingdom of Hungary—defeated in the First World War, then dismantled, degraded and now disappeared—lives on in this mysterious and glorious object. One of Europe’s oldest surviving crowns, with a lower section of enamel imagery dating all the way back to medieval Byzantium, it likely took on its present appearance in the 12th century. Containing both Latin and Greek inscriptions, and bejeweled with sapphires, garnets and amethysts, the elaborate golden crown had mystical status. It was not only a symbol, but treated as the actual incarnation of the Hungarian state, and sovereigns were not regarded as rulers until it was placed on their heads.

A miraculous survivor of Hungary’s cataclysmic 20th century, it was brought back into use in 1990 following the collapse of communism. Placed on Hungary’s newly devised coat of arms, it has been on display in the national parliament since 2000.

Lili Ország’s Wall of Icons II (Blue) (1969).

Hungarian National GallerySzent György térNow regarded as one of the most notable artists to emerge in Hungary after the Second World War, Ország, born into a Hungarian Jewish family in what is now Ukraine, barely escaped being deported to Auschwitz and later survived the war as a Christian convert.

Judaism, Christianity, and her own biography fuse together in her mature paintings, whose religious elements were in defiance of official communist policies. This late piece, showing a repeating Madonna-and-Child motif, is part of a series of oil-on-fiberboard works. Invoking her longstanding interest in Orthodox Christian imagery, it also alludes to her own trauma at not having had a child.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareGoya’s transition from a designer of Rococo tapestries to the great harbinger of Modernism is on view in this legendary painting, made during the dark years of Napoleonic Spain's Peninsular War, a guerrilla conflict that foreshadowed the atrocities of the 20th century.

An apparent genre scene showing a rustic girl carrying food and water, the painting is in fact a wartime vision of desperate heroism. The late art critic Robert Hughes was fascinated by the work, which he regarded as an “emblem of resistance.” He writes, in his 2003 biography of the artist: “You would be very grateful to see her if you were crouched stiffly behind a rock in the parching autumn sun of Aragón, breathing hot dust with the ricochets whining above.”.

Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial.

Can Togay and Gyula Pauer’s Shoes on the Danube Bank (2005)Id. Antall József rkpIn the years after the collapse of communism in 1989, the newly open societies of Central and Eastern Europe revisited the horrors of their 20th century in a number of commemorative works. This installation on the banks of the Danube, which memorialises the victims of the predominantly anti-Semitic massacres by Hungary’s fascist militias in 1944-45, is now considered one of the most artistically successful.

Comprising 60 pairs of rusty iron shoes, it was devised by Togay, a filmmaker, and executed together with Pauer, a performance artist and sculptor. Fixed in concrete but eerily scattered, the shoes—in women’s, men’s, and children’s sizes and styles—recall the militia's orders of its victims to remove their shoes before shooting them into the river.

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939).

© Museum of Fine Arts – Vasarely Museum, Budapest.

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939)Vasarely Museum BudapestSzentlélek térFor the first few decades of the 20th century, Budapest was a hothouse of the avant-garde, nurturing the likes of Modernist painter László Moholy-Nagy; Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer; and the supreme chronicler of 1930s Paris, photographer Gyula Halász, otherwise known as Brassaï. Their work is hard to find back in Budapest, but their near contemporary, Victor Vasarely, the great pioneer of Op Art, has his own museum here.

Schooled in Modernist trends in a Budapest private art academy, Vasarely decamped for Paris in 1930, and his experiments there in the late 1930s anticipated Op Art’s illusions and manipulations by some three decades. This tempera-on-paper work was a stand-out at this year's survey of the artist, Vasarely 120, held at MFAB. It is considered a great forerunner of the movement, which Vasarely went on to promote, often in ever-larger formats, until his death in 1997, aged 90.

Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

In a recent development, pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ Square.

Industry observers note that hungary’s longtime Habsburg rulers, residing up the Danube in Vienna, began amassing their unique collection of works by Pieter Bruegel the Elder within decades of his death in 1569. But this late work somehow got past them, ending up in the Hungarian collection of the noble Batthyány family.

Sources indicate that A vast social panorama, with a solemnity largely missing from the artist’s more raucous works, the painting depicts nobles and soldiers, burghers and peasants, Jews and Turks, the healthy and the infirm. Nearly all are transfixed and transformed by the teachings of Christ, as spoken by St. John the Baptist, who is illuminated by little more than the attention of the crowd.

Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996).

Photo © József Rosta / Ludwig Museum - MoCA, Budapest.

© SUMUS Gáyor & Maurer Foundation.

Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996)Ludwig MuseumKomor Marcell utcaDuring the Orbán years, Budapest’s large national art institutions took on a retrograde atmosphere, with leading artists, like their emerging counterparts, often resorting to alternative or municipal venues. Paradoxically, it coincided with an international breakthrough of some cutting-edge figures, like Maurer, who had a 2019 survey at London’s Tate Modern.

A trained graphic artist, Maurer was eventually drawn to geometric abstraction and witty illusionism. This mature acrylic-on-wood piece, acquired by the Ludwig Museum in 1998, uses lines on an apparently curved surface to create a near-sculptural, if resolutely two-dimensional piece.

Black timber elements traverse concrete fragrance store in Tokyo

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (382 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.
  • Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.
  • The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Takuya Yamauchi.

Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.

Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.

The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.

“We approached the project as an intervention within an existing building, rather than simply designing an interior,” mentioned Esrawe Studio founder Héctor Esrawe, who also co-founded Xinú.

“By introducing a continuous architectural structure that traverses its different levels, appearing and disappearing throughout the volume, we intended to generate a latest perception of the original architecture,” he told Dezeen.

“Both structures coexist, establishing a dialogue between what was already there and what has been introduced, creating an unexpected spatial experience.”.

Long, overlapping shelves with mirrored accents display products on the ground floor, which is dedicated to body perfume.

Xinú’s room scents are located on the first floor, where hand-painted brass panels on the walls and ceilings add a touch of warmth to the concrete and black-timber surfaces.

Aiming to reveal the processes behind the perfume products, the top floor displays botanical specimens, raw materials, found objects and collages in drawers.

Esrawe Studio also designed cabinet drawers to reference the storage and organisation typically found in natural history museums, intending to give visitors a feeling of discovery when interacting with the furniture.

“For Xinú, architecture has never been conceived simply as a backdrop for products, but as an essential part of how they are experienced,” remarked Esrawe.

“Our intention is to create spaces that encourage curiosity, discovery and a more intimate relationship with objects, materials and scent,” he continued.

“In Tokyo, the inserted architectural structures move beyond conventional retail display, becoming sculptural elements that enhance the presence of the objects.”.

It has been revealed that xinú Tokyo is the latest branch Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts have designed for the perfume brand. Other shops include a radial wooden pavilion in Mexico City and a showroom in Oaxaca informed by basalt rock formations.

Photography by Takuya Yamauchi.

#103581. Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1438 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • India’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November.
  • According to recent reports, the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for substantial works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses.
  • Industry observers note that for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

India’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers said that a date clash with Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to most local exhibitors selling around half, rather than all their stands.

According to recent reports, the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for substantial works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).

Industry observers note that for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” said Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand—including photographs by the Kolkata-based filmmaker Ronny Sen referencing post-humanism—and rehung around 50% of it.

Notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a upcoming buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.

In a recent development, in the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.

Subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send out PDFs to its clients prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” said the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.

Art Mumbai takes place at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse.

With India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox stated this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.

Recent findings suggest that also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that revealed at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (New York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).

Several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. On the closing day, gallery director Ellie Harrison-Read said that she had a "good fair, but closing a few more sales could make it great”.

Industry observers note that by and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works struggled. Niru Ratnam, which revealed small paintings in muted palettes by the late Bengali-British Modernist Amal Ghosh and the British Indian Bhajan Hunjan, did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Ghosh to cover stand and shipping costs.

According to recent reports, while both Ghosh and Hunjan are increasingly being reappraised by world leading institutions such as Tate, they are relatively unknown figures in both the UK and India and have proved a tough sell in Mumbai. As one local dealer noted, "I rarely meet collectors here who lead with curiosity or instinct".

Another litmus test for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff said she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.

The gallery did however sell to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art a $16,000 painting installation by Divya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff noted.

Speaking of Picasso, a 1930s painting by the Spanish master was offered by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery demonstrated a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, gallery director Hugo Cobb decided to double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he remarked.

The gallery did not sell the Picasso by the end of the fair, with Cobb attesting to the fact that the very top end of the Indian market still amounts to a handful of collectors. "There are maybe four or five collectors in this country who would buy it, and none of them did." The gallery did, however, sell a monumentally scaled Yoan Capote painting, embedded with fishhooks, for $1m to a local collector. Cobb added that should the gallery return to Art Mumbai, it will focus on bringing high value secondary market material.

Sources indicate that as many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes remain local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by familiarity," says the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff.".

Sources indicate that further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes involved in shipping works in and out of the country. As the Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan said, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in art. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".

Meanwhile, concerns of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one adviser, speaking anonymously, noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".

It has been revealed that india's art market growth indeed appears to be a domestic success story. This is in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.

While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, many collectors covet international—usually Western—names at the expense of local talent, India overwhelmingly supports its own artists: representatives from a growing number of newly introduced Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.

While India might not yet be ready for a truly international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which should help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer period.

Giga Unveils the AD Italia redesign

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Giga rebuilds AD Italia for its 45th anniversary: the AD Italia redesign pairs Arizona type, Ghirri colour and a modernist grid.
  • The first thing you see is the masthead.
  • Arizona, by Dinamo Typefaces, is almost a sans with flared strokes, and it brings the measure of Roman inscriptions to the page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giga rebuilds AD Italia for its 45th anniversary: the AD Italia redesign pairs Arizona type, Ghirri colour and a modernist grid.

The first thing you see is the masthead. AD sits in black flared serif on a soft pink field, the letters drawn wide enough to carry the cover on their own, and the same confidence runs through the matter. Inside, the November pages open on a white field with SPAZI set large in the same face, issue N.530, and the spreads that follow give each photograph a full page of air. The palette stays soft and everyday: coral, pale green and pale blue, the colours of an Italian landscape rather than a brand manual.

Proportion went to the type. Arizona, by Dinamo Typefaces, is almost a sans with flared strokes, and it brings the measure of Roman inscriptions to the page. A specimen page sets names in Arizona Flare Light, one per line, with nothing else on the field, and the same face carries the cover lines: SPAZI across a white cover, LA NOSTRA GUIDA AL SALONE 2025 stacked in white on black. The letters do the talking, and the layout stays out of their way.

Essentiality went to the grid. Giga built it on the logic of modern art catalogues: photographs get room of their own, captions stay small and precise, and the editorial pages stand apart from the advertising around them. A spread on David Bowie runs green panels beside a column of text that starts in 1972, when Bowie became Ziggy Stardust, and a grid of anniversary spreads collects 45 icons from the magazine's history on a single page.

Colour went to Luigi Ghirri. The case page sets the palette beside three everyday Italian landscapes, a canal road, green houses against the sea, a beach with swings, all in the soft register of Ghirri's photographs. The system names its colours plainly: PMS 2344 C coral, PMS 2260 C pale green, PMS 290 C pale blue, each with its hex code printed beside it, the way a printer would want it.

Wit went to the rhythm. Like Ettore Sottsass's Carlton bookcase, which slants its shelves and still holds books, the system plays with its own conventions, varying titles and images from story to story. The redesign launched with the November 2026 issue and a room at PAC Milano built around one line: perfect proportions, essential function, a joke, the colours of every day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

French architecture studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel has shared photos revealing construction progress on the giant Shenzhen Opera House, due for completion in China in 2028.

Located on the Shekou Peninsula overlooking Shenzhen Bay, the opera house will eventually be defined by an elongated, wavy roofscape, nodding to the site’s connection to the sea.

Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel’s studio has designed it as a fresh cultural landmark for the city, with a 2,300-seat concert hall, an 1,800-seat theatre and an 800-seat venue among its facilities.

The construction photos help visualise the scale of the 250,000-square-metre opera house, with its various facilities sprawling out across its waterfront site.

They showcase its main concert hall with its horseshoe-shaped strategy, alongside the two smaller performance venues.

Ateliers Jean Nouvel’s design for Shenzhen Opera House was the winning entry of an invited international architecture competition, for which other entrants included SIGNIFICANT, Snøhetta, MVRDV and Kengo Kuma.

Alongside the main performance halls, it will contain a multifunctional theatre with 400 seats, cultural spaces, backstage areas, apartments for performers and offices.

To help further connect the building to the surrounding water, the interior is expected to feature iridescent materials such as mother-of-pearl, also known as nacre.

“The sea will be both around you and over you,” explained Nouvel when the project was revealed in 2021.

“This explains more clearly why the main foyer has to be made of a noble, precious and luminous material that spells the meeting of sea and music and light,” Nouvel continued.

“Using the lustrous white reflections of a nacreous material will be a concrete poeticisation of the meeting of the sea and the auditorium and concert halls of the Opera House.”.

French architect Nouvel founded his eponymous studio in 1994. We recently reported on the news that the studio’s La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed with Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos, was damaged in a fire. The project won the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards, which took place last night.

Another landmark opera house recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Grand Opera House, designed by Snøhetta with a giant spiral staircase.

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel.
